Mary Heilmann obituary
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-20
16:50:35 UTC
01:50:35 KST

Visitors to Mary Heilmann’s show at the Whitechapel Gallery in 2016 were offered the novel experience of looking at art while scooting about on wheeled wooden chairs. These, too, turned out to be artworks. One, Sunny Chair for the Whitechapel, had been made by Heilmann for the occasion. Rough-hewn from plywood, backed in nylon webbing and painted bright yellow, it seemed happily untidy; as an object, but also as a type. This was true of all the works in Looking at Pictures, and was intentional.
Heilmann, who has died aged 86, had an untidy past as a maker. It was while doing a BA at the University of California, Santa Barbara (1959-62), that she discovered ceramics, which were to occupy her first decade as an artist. The untidiness of her artistic history, however, was to be shaped by more than her choice of materials.
Born in San Francisco, she was the daughter of John, a civil engineer, and Mary (nee Webb), a nurse. Her mother had insisted on continuing to work while raising her two children. She instilled the need for self-sufficiency into her daughter, who trained as a teacher before going to art school.
When Heilmann was seven, her family moved south to Los Angeles. The city’s surf culture attracted her, particularly diving. “I became a fledgling competitive diver at 11,” she told the Guardian in an interview for her Whitechapel show. “A little girl could get a lot of attention diving off the tower at the Coliseum.” As she would discover, though, attention was harder to come by as a female artist.
In 1965, she signed on to a ceramics and sculpture MA at Berkeley, taught by the celebrated ceramicist Peter Voulkos. “He was amazing,” Heilmann recalled. “A super-radical nut-job hippie.”
Voulkos’s huge, abstract expressionist ceramics were on the scale of sculpture, although he had initially trained as a painter. His student would now go the other way, exchanging ceramics for sculpture and then, by the late 1960s, painting.
For all that, Heilmann did not get the kind of attention she had had as a high-board diver, or that male friends such as Bruce Nauman and Richard Serra were now getting as students. “It was the case that girls were very not noticed as artists,” she told an Archives of American Art interviewer in 2022. “There were a lot of really good young women artists, but only a few got any attention.”
This, in part, is what drove her to untidiness. If teachers such as Voulkos overlooked her and her work, she would get their attention “not by being sexy and cute and flirty, but by being provocative and ornery, and then making art that was provocative and ornery”.
In 1968, Heilmann left California for New York, intent on meeting the minimalist artist Donald Judd. (Judd too had made chairs, although his “were not very comfortable”, Heilmann told Vogue magazine. “Mine are.”) Moving into Serra’s former loft in Manhattan’s Tribeca, she was visited by Holly Solomon, a dealer whose eponymous gallery specialised in the work of Californian artists. From 1976, Solomon gave Heilmann a series of shows. The third, in 1979, was a flop.
The problem was pink. In her desire to be ornery, Heilmann had made a series of paintings that defied the colour’s association with femininity – “fluffy dress pink”, as she called it. “Pink is a pretty colour,” Heilmann said, “but it was also a hip, culturally hip, naughty colour, or a rough, rough colour.”
The one she used for her paintings in the 1979 show was assertively naughty and rough – an acid, eye-popping pink offset in each canvas by black. The works, Heilmann said, may have been “playful and sarcastic”, but they were also “very, very serious, and formal, and colourist”, informed by the thinking of the Bauhaus colour theorist Josef Albers. This fact eluded the critic of the Village Voice, who sniffed that the canvases lacked “real muscle”, and that Heilmann “hadn’t been doing her push-ups”. What made this borderline misogynistic attack particularly painful was that the critic was a woman.
Leaving Holly Solomon soon after, Heilmann went to the gallerist Pat Hearn, who gave her a series of exhibitions throughout the late 80s and 90s.
Her life changed when, in 1997, she was taken up by the Swiss kingmakers, Hauser & Wirth. In that year, she had her first international one-woman exhibition in Zurich, at the Zürcher Stiftung für Konstruktive und Konkrete Kunst. A solo show at the Camden Art Centre in London followed in 2001, and at the Museum Ludwig in Cologne in 2010.
Through all of this, Heilmann and her art proved resistant to tidiness. The earliest pieces in her Whitechapel show, such as Little 9 x 9 (1973), were finger paintings, a method Heilmann had learned when teaching children. She would have a longer career teaching adults, at Stony Brook University on Long Island and then at the School of Visual Arts in Manhattan. “I made the work by squeezing through the paint with my fingers,” she said.
Black Cracky (1990) showed a fascination with breakage, a relic of her life as a ceramicist. That she saw the canvas as an object rather than just a surface – sides and stretcher bars were also painted – she ascribed to having been a sculptor. Her paintings were sculptures, as were her chairs. The blobs that seemed to fly up the gallery wall from the double canvas of Good Vibrations Diptych, Remembering David (2012) recalled “a time in the 60s, the hippy era, when people saw spots flying around due to certain substances that were also flying around,” Heilmann cryptically said.
That she had indulged in those substances herself was just one of her untidinesses. She had, she said, dried out in 1983, although titles of works such as Surfing on Acid (2005) suggested a lingering fascination with the beach and the counterculture it bred. Given all this, her attitude to Catholicism was perhaps even more surprising.
Brought up in a devoutly Catholic household – her brother trained as a priest – she had been sent to schools with names such as the St Rose academy and American Martyrs. The experience never left her. “I loved the whole Catholic culture as a kid, and that’s carried on into my life, the way I make things up now,” she told the documentary channel Art21 in 2009. Her 1983 painting Rosebud was a meditation on the martyrdom of St Sebastian. Another canvas was called Our Lady of the Flowers.
Heilmann spent her last years in Bridgehampton, Long Island. Her brother, John, predeceased her. She is survived by his three children.

Charity campaigner’s death in microlight crash was accidental, coroner rules
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-20
16:49:04 UTC
01:49:04 KST

The death of a disability campaigner after a microlight crash while filming a TV programme for Apple was an accident, a coroner has concluded.
An inquest heard on Thursday that Claire Lomas, 44, died of severe traumatic injuries on 22 August 2024, five weeks after a light aircraft she had been piloting while filming a series to promote Apple’s Vision Pro headset “veered off the runway” during a landing operation and crashed into a rock in Amman, Jordan.
After becoming paralysed from the waist down in a horse-riding accident in 2007, Lomas, from Leicestershire, became a charity campaigner. She raised more than £900,000 for the Nicholls Spinal Injury Foundation and was the first person to finish a marathon with the aid of a “bionic” suit when she completed the 2012 London Marathon in 17 days.
The inquest heard that the Royal Aero Sports Club of Jordan had concluded there was no violation of ground or air safety procedures, and that there was no evidence the 180-degree camera attached to the aircraft had adversely affected the flight.
Concerns about Lomas’s confidence to fly the microlight were explored during the hearing. Ben Ashman, a microlight designer whose company built an adapted version of the aircraft to allow Lomas to fly without the use of her feet, said he believed Lomas may have been stressed before the flight because she posted on Facebook about putting her “brave pants” on, which he said was unusual for her.
Louise Pinder, the senior coroner for Rutland and North Leicestershire, recorded Lomas’s death as accidental, telling the hearing she “was involved in the filming of an episode of Adventure which formed part of a series designed for a virtual reality headset”.
Pinder added: “During the final approach to the roadway, where she was to land, it became apparent to her and to those on the ground that the aircraft was not perfectly aligned.
“Claire made a split-second decision to abort the landing and go around but the aircraft touched down firmly, veered to the left, the left wheel leaving the road on to gravel causing her to further lose control. The aircraft collided with rocks approximately 10 metres from the metalled road surface, as a result of which she sustained multiple traumatic injuries.”
Pinder added: “I have heard no evidence establishing a causal link between any deficiencies in the risk assessment and Claire’s death. I am reassured, as I hope the family will be, that there have been thorough investigations as far as possible into the circumstances of Claire’s death and some lessons have been learnt.”
Pinder noted that Lomas’s family had raised concerns about the quality of care she received in hospital in Jordan, but said there was insufficient evidence to conclude whether there were any missed opportunities in her treatment.
Katherine Allen, a lawyer speaking on behalf of the Lomas family, said the inquest’s conclusion marked “the end of a very difficult, emotional process” for them and that “the family continue to live with the devastating consequences of their loss”.
“Claire was deeply loved and her death has left a profound and enduring void in their lives,” Allen said in a statement. “They will never be the same again following what happened to her.”

"We will not tolerate a Turkish military entrenchment moving southward, because it threatens us," Netanyahu told an army radio podcast.
The premier's office also said on Tuesday evening that Israel had repeatedly warned Syria that deploying Turkish forces at an airbase near Aleppo would pose a threat to its national security, noting that Damascus had ignored the warnings.
The office stated that Israel and Syria had agreed to maintain the status quo on security matters, claiming that Damascus was on the verge of violating this understanding by allowing the Turkish military deployment.
But Turkish defence ministry spokesman Rear Admiral Zeki Akturk said the strikes were "unacceptable" and that Ankara would act "resolutely" to protect Syria's efforts to establish post-war stability.
"Israel's attack on the Abu al-Zuhur air base is aimed at harming Syria's stability, security, unity, integrity and infrastructure. Attacks violating Syria's sovereignty and territorial integrity are unacceptable," he told journalists.
"In this context, our efforts and contributions to protect Syria's sovereignty and territorial integrity, and help it establish a stable and secure environment, will continue resolutely."
Turkey’s presidency has also clarified that it is not considering retaliation.
Duran said that Netanyahu was "clinging to this irrational stance due to upcoming elections, internal political tensions, and fears. He views hostility toward Turkey as a political lifeline".
The development comes as Syria’s new transitional government has condemned the Israeli strikes, which marked the first time the location was targeted since the fall of the Assad regime.
The US has also rebuked the strikes, with US special envoy to Syria Tom Barrack describing the attack as an "unnecessary escalation" that did not serve regional stability.
Barrack pointed to the approach taken by the government of Syrian President Ahmed al-Sharaa, saying Damascus "has not adopted a hostile posture nor maintained proxy forces, but has repeatedly demonstrated a preference for de-escalation with Israel".
He also emphasised Washington's efforts to reduce tensions between the two countries.
Barrack called on all sides to prioritise "reasoned dialogue" over further military incidents.
Since the fall of the Assad regime, Israel has stepped up its raids and incursions into Syria, while targeting much of the country's remaining military infrastructure.
Israeli attacks have struck Syrian air-defence systems, long- and medium-range missiles, weapons and missile depots, scientific research centres and other military facilities.
Israeli strikes have also hit several key Syrian airfields and military installations, including Hama airport, as well as Tiyas, Shayrat, Palmyra, Dumayr and Mezzeh airfields.
Agencies contributed to this report.

Lack of low-carbon power could deter investment
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-20
16:46:39 UTC
01:46:39 KST

Taiwan’s shortage of readily available low-carbon electricity could deter investment in artificial intelligence (AI) data centers despite the country’s technological strengths, a renewable energy executive said yesterday.
AI data centers require more than electricity: They need power that is available around the clock, scalable, affordable, low-carbon and deliverable within their development timelines, INA Energy Corp (寶晶能源) chairman Norman Tsai (蔡佳?) said at an energy transition forum in Taipei.
Large facilities can require between 50 megawatts and several hundred megawatts of power, with some reaching gigawatt scale, Tsai said.
Photo: CNA
The required power infrastructure must also be available quickly because data centers can be completed within 12 to 24 months, while new transmission lines or substations often take five to 10 years, he said.
“To achieve firm power, you need what I would call a combined approach,” Tsai said. “It involves not only power generation, but also the grid.”
“Taiwan is technologically strong, but it lacks sources of electricity, and that is why AI data centers are reluctant to establish operations here,” he said.
More specifically, Taiwan lacks green electricity, Tsai said, adding that identifying an adequate low-carbon power source would be the first challenge facing an AI date center operator seeking to establish a facility in the nation.
Citing the International Energy Agency, Tsai’s presentation said global data center electricity demand was projected to rise from 485 terawatt-hours (TWh) last year to 950TWh in 2030.
Corporate demand for green electricity is also spreading through the semiconductor supply chain because one company’s emissions from purchased energy, known as Scope 2 emissions, become part of its customers’ indirect Scope 3 emissions, Tsai said.
As a result, major Taiwanese semiconductor companies are helping their suppliers purchase or invest in green power, he added.
European Economic and Trade Office trade section head Christoph Saurenbach told the forum that Taiwan and the EU face similar difficulties reconciling decarbonization with industrial competitiveness.
Taiwan’s challenges are compounded by its geographic and geopolitical position and its heavy reliance on imported fossil fuels, he said.
The green transition is not only an economic and environmental necessity for Taiwan, but also “a strategic and political and security necessity,” Saurenbach said.
Rapidly expanding AI and semiconductor industries would make the transition more difficult and require greater investment and support from those sectors, he added.
European companies are major investors in Taiwan’s offshore wind sector, giving the EU and Taiwan a shared interest in the success of the nation’s renewable energy transition, Saurenbach said.
He also cited the Strait of Hormuz crisis as demonstrating the risks of long-term dependence on imported energy.
“Investment in renewables really is an obligation,” Saurenbach said. “There are absolutely no alternatives.”

Defense autonomy at risk if drone budget is stalled
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-20
16:46:37 UTC
01:46:37 KST

Forcing drone procurement into the annual budget cycle could cripple Taiwan’s defense autonomy and deter the domestic drone industry from investing in crucial “non-red” supply chains, a national security official said yesterday, following a breakdown in negotiations over a special budget for uncrewed systems.
Earlier in the day, the Legislative Yuan’s Economics Committee failed to reconcile 14 versions of a special budget bill to fund the domestic development of surveillance and combat drones.
The opposition Chinese Nationalist Party (KMT) and Taiwan People’s Party disagreed with the Executive Yuan placing large uncrewed vehicle orders in a special budget and prioritizing military systems over those for civilian use.
Photo: Tu Chien-jung, Taipei Times
The national security official, speaking on condition of anonymity, said that high-volume government orders, not empty platitudes, are needed for Taiwan to develop its drone-making industry.
Drone technology is rapidly advancing and a generation of uncrewed systems could become obsolete in a little more than a month, they said.
Maintaining the tempo of research and development to sustain battlefield relevance requires the industry to have confidence in government funding, which can only be provided through high-volume orders, rather than through annual budgets that fluctuate, the official said.
Under the circumstances, it comes as no surprise that big contracts and a focus on military applications have become the global paradigm for developing drone technology, they said.
Washington’s Replicator Initiative to obtain thousands of low-cost autonomous systems, which has counterparts in Japan, South Korea and the EU, exemplify that approach, the official said.
Orders for coastal surveillance drones, coastal attack drones and maritime loitering munitions are carefully designed to provide the military with mission-critical capabilities, they said.
Altering the number of systems in the orders or changing the delivery timetable would cause worrisome delays in the government’s force-building plans, they added.
The government designed the military contracts for drones to focus on stability and concentration of effort, which include acquiring weapon systems, maintenance and repair capabilities, as well as institutional knowledge, the official said.
The Cabinet’s plan to buy drones with a special budget is intended to establish the capability to mass-produce uncrewed systems without crowding out other essential government programs, they said.
High-volume manufacturing is a crucial aspect of drone warfare, given the scale needed in wartime, they said, adding that Taiwan especially needs self-sufficient drone-making capability to counter a potential naval blockade by China.
National security and economic interests are aligned on drones, instead of being in competition as the opposition party suggests, the official added.

Hyrox chases Olympic dream amid soaring popularity
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-20
16:46:36 UTC
01:46:36 KST

From about 650 competitors at its first event to more than 1 million participants worldwide today, Hyrox has gone from niche fitness challenge to global phenomenon with its sights set on the Olympics in less than a decade.
A structured indoor activity divided into eight segments, each involving a 1km run followed by a fitness exercise, Hyrox attracts tens of thousands of participants to its biggest events.
Its mix of stop-start runs, easy-to-learn exercises, competition and community has proved popular with everyone from elite athletes to everyday exercisers, and organizers believe the sky is the limit in terms of growth.
Photo: AP
“We have close to 1.5 million people at some stage this year participating in our events,” Hyrox’s India head Deepak Raj said.
“We’re in 35-plus countries, 100-plus cities and each of the events are getting bigger in participation levels,” he said
“It’s hard to put a ceiling [on it] when we know that there are gyms where some people haven’t even done a Hyrox, or haven’t maybe even heard of it in some countries,” he said.
Hyrox was developed in 2017 by Christian Toetzke and Moritz Fuerste, who won hockey gold medals for Germany in the 2008 and 2012 Summer Olympics.
The prospect of it being included in the Olympics is not just wishful thinking, after World Triathlon approved the format under the name “Hyathlon” this year.
While Raj said it was too soon to make a case for the sport’s inclusion in 2028, they are aiming for a spot on the program of the 2032 and 2036 Games.
“In the world championships earlier this year in Stockholm, we had 101 countries represented. It has become a global sport. Standards have been established,” Raj said.
“The 2028 Olympics was obviously a little too soon, given the sport had not yet caught on to several regions and countries. But 2032 and 2036, that is the pathway or the goal,” he said.
For this year’s world champion Alyssa McElheny, competing at the Olympics would be a dream come true.
“I know that it’s still a few years off. There’s some more standardization of the sport that has to happen before that dream can be possible,” the American distance runner said.
“But I do think it would be a sport that fits really well in the Olympics. It’s something that doesn’t really exist out there currently,” she said.
Hyrox has been life-changing for McElheny, allowing her to leave the wedding photography business and pursue the sport full-time.
A runner who clocked 2:34:28 in Indianapolis to also qualify for US Olympic marathon trials, her success in the emerging sport has brought with it an Adidas sponsorship.
“If you had told me this time last year that I’d be sponsored by Adidas for a sport that wasn’t marathoning, I would have been like, ‘What are you talking about?’” the 35-year-old said.
“I have just two weddings left to photograph now and then after that, I’m a full-time athlete... We’re going to see more of that [full sponsorships] in the near future, the sport is growing,” she said.
Asian markets comprise a significant portion of Hyrox’s growth, with India hosting five events this season and expecting about 50,000 participants as organizers look to increase the size and duration of races.
“For us, the venue infrastructure and size is going to be a limiting factor about where we can host it, so our goal is to make existing events larger,” Raj said.
“Bangalore was a two-day event this year, next year it’s going to be a five-day event,” he said.
“We believe we could have anywhere between maybe eight to 10 cities [in India] hosting Hyrox, and each of the races being at least three to four days,” he said.

Hualien researchers tout seedling production work
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-20
16:46:34 UTC
01:46:34 KST

The Hualien District Agricultural Research and Extension Station has developed cutting propagation and seedling production techniques for makauy to address short supplies of the indigenous plant by boosting its germination rate to 70 percent.
Makauy, also known as Taiwan mountain pepper (Litsea cubeba), is a perennial plant with fruit that has lemon, pepper and pine aromas.
It is a native aromatic spice often used by indigenous people that has become popular in the domestic market.
Photo: Liu Pin-chuan, Taipei Times
However, the industry has faced a shortage of seedlings, as the plant is difficult to propagate, the station said.
After many years, it has boosted the plant’s germination rate to 70 percent, it said.
In 2023, the station informed the Sioulin Township (秀林) Office of the technique, leading to a bountiful harvest this year, it said.
The office last year named makauy as one of the township’s “three treasures” alongside pigeon pea and red quinoa, showing that the crop has become important to the local agricultural industry, it said.
Station researchers regularly visit the township to inspect makauy cultivation and reported that most of the plants are more than 2m tall, it said.
The results show that the township’s soil and climate is suited for growing makauy, the station said.
A local grower told the station that production used to be unstable, as the crop was rarely found in the wild.
However, production has stabilized within only two years since the station shared the technique, the grower said, adding that green makauy fruits cover the hillside near his home.
The station said the technique is expected to resolve the seedling shortage and provide indigenous communities with stable incomes.
Makauy is dioecious, meaning that only its female plants produce flowers and bear fruit.
Given that it is difficult to identify whether a makauy plant is male or female at its seedling stage, the station has conducted cutting propagation trials to produce high-quality female plants via asexual propagation, the station said.
Standardizing the technique effectively controlled the male-to-female ratio of seedlings, ensuring that most plants grown by local farmers are female, it said.
The method has significantly increased makauy yields per unit area in indigenous communities, it added.
The station said it has also been researching makauy by-products.
Leaves and flower buds of the plant were collected during different seasons and from different areas to compare essential oil extraction efficiency, it said.
The goal is to develop processed makauy products for the township’s Taroko communities while balancing sustainable resource use with ecological restoration, the station said.

Experts weigh in on fate of Control, Examination yuans
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-20
16:46:34 UTC
01:46:34 KST

Experts at a meeting of the legislature’s Constitutional Amendment Committee yesterday advocated abolishing the Control Yuan and Examination Yuan to transition to a bicameral system, while others warned of unconstitutional overreach.
National Chengchi University College of Law professor Lin Chai-ho (林佳和) told the Legislative Yuan committee that while oversight powers are necessary, the Control Yuan itself was not.
However, a constitutional amendment would be required to abolish the Control Yuan, he said.
Photo: Tu Chien-jung, Taipei Times
With the abolishment of the National Assembly in the process of Taiwan’s democratization, the Control Yuan is in direct competition with the Legislative Yuan’s investigation powers, Lin said.
The Control Yuan could be merged into the legislature, but that would require a system of procedural guarantees and the establishment of new committees, while ensuring the power of impeachment is exercised with caution, he said.
Lin suggested establishing a “parliamentary ombudsman” and separating the National Human Rights Council from the Control Yuan under the Paris Principles.
National Sun Yat-sen University political economy professor Jang Chyi-lu (張其祿), a former Taiwan People’s Party legislator-at-large, suggested turning the Control Yuan into something like an upper house of the legislature tasked with audits, policy reviews, upholding human rights, holding legislative investigations, and issuing recalls and corrections.
The total number of legislative seats could be increased to 180, with 100 seats going to the lower house for regional legislators, and the upper house formed by 34 legislators-at-large, combined with 29 members of the oversight committee, plus 17 new seats, he said.
Attorney Hong Wei-sheng (洪偉勝) said that despite the Examination Yuan’s purpose to prevent fraud, experience with entrance examinations shows that ensuring fairness does not necessarily require independent state power, adding that the civil-service system should consider recruiting private-sector talent.
Should the power of oversight be returned to the Legislative Yuan, the National Human Rights Commission should become independent, he said.
The number of seats and internal checks and balances of the legislature should be reviewed, as the current 113 seats are insufficient, he added.
Democracy Foundation CEO Kuei Hung-chen (桂宏誠) said the Examination Yuan’s value lies in maintaining professionalism and neutrality.
The politicization of civil servants and the corruption of contract employees is already a problem, but the abolishment of the Examination Yuan could further politicize the Executive Yuan and civil servants, Kuei said.
Taiwan Public Policy Association president Chi Chun-chen (紀俊臣) said that according to Constitutional Interpretation No. 499, the separation of powers and checks and balances fall under the scope of constitutional drafting, not constitutional amendment.
Abolishing the Examination Yuan and the Control Yuan is inappropriate, he said, adding that the Examination Yuan should remain independent to maintain a fair promotion system.

====================================================================================================

Film review: The Day the War Ended
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-20
16:46:33 UTC
01:46:33 KST

They were born Taiwanese, educated as Japanese and drawn into the war effort for an empire that was eventually defeated. Under the Chinese Nationalist Party (KMT) regime, when Japanese became the enemy, they mostly kept those memories to themselves.
Of the six men and women interviewed in depth for The Day the War Ended (終戰那一天), three have since died, while the others are nearing 100. Their stories are therefore all the more urgent to preserve, offering an invaluable glimpse into what Taiwanese went through during a period of great change.
With Taiwan’s current representative to Finland, Freddy Lim (林昶佐), narrating and conducting the interviews, the film connects their experiences to the present, reflecting on how Taiwan’s turbulent past continues to affect its people today. It’s a deeply sympathetic look at a difficult time in Taiwan’s history, bringing to light nuances and contradictions about that period that are often overlooked.
Photo courtesy of Activator Marketing Corp
Born in the 1920s, the six subjects came of age during Japan’s Kominka period, when the colonial government sought to assimilate Taiwanese into loyal imperial subjects. Society became increasingly militarized after the Second Sino-Japanese War broke out in 1937, and more than 200,000 Taiwanese served the Japanese military during World War II, first as noncombatant workers and later as soldiers. Over 30,000 died.
As the film shows, they experienced the war in different ways and for different reasons. Some joined for better pay, some volunteered for non-combat positions because they expected to be drafted anyway, some went under societal pressure and some genuinely believed it was their duty to serve Japan. And those who did not participate also felt the war up close.
The six follow markedly different paths. Tung Chun-hsien (東俊賢) headed to Japan at age 13 or 14 to train as a mechanic to work on military aircraft, including planes intended for kamikaze missions, while Lee Chien-chiao (李遷嬌) went to Hong Kong and Guangzhou as a nursing assistant. Yang Fu-cheng (楊馥成) and Hsiao Chin-wen (蕭錦文), meanwhile, both saw action in Southeast Asia as, respectively, a military auxiliary and volunteer soldier.
Late democracy activist and politician Peng Ming-min (彭明敏) avoided joining the Japanese military while studying in Tokyo because he was opposed to war and identified with China at the time. He sought refuge near Nagasaki with his brother, only to witness the atomic bombing from outside the city. Huang Chin-kui (黃金桂) was still a student and was in Taiwan during the Allied bombings. Despite their differing journeys, all six witnessed the horrors and upheaval of the war, which they discuss candidly in the film.
As the KMT took over Taiwan, those experiences became taboo to discuss. Many Taiwanese initially welcomed the end of colonial rule and expected to be accepted as first-class citizens, but instead they were viewed with suspicion and, in many cases, mistreated once more. Some Taiwanese who had served Japan or were sympathetic to it could be branded as traitors or collaborators, leaving little room for the complexities of their lived realities and feelings.
Director Maxine Lu (盧慈穎) noted at the premiere that she grew up largely oblivious to the war her grandparents had lived through, even believing that Taiwan had been bombed by the Japanese rather than the Allies.
“I was not interested in learning more about it because I was repeatedly told that Taiwan was absent from this war,” she said.
The film avoids romanticizing Japanese colonial rule. Discrimination and second-class treatment existed alongside the infrastructure and modernization the colonizers brought, while some Taiwanese developed a genuine sense of allegiance to Japan and formed friendships with their Japanese neighbors. It does not treat these realities as mutually exclusive.
Nor does it shy away from Japan’s wartime atrocities, including the Nanjing Massacre, providing context for the KMT’s animosity toward Japan after the war. It also touches on the postwar tragedies that followed, including abuses by KMT soldiers, the 228 Incident and the White Terror. By placing all of these experiences within the same historical frame, the film further highlights the fact that history is never black and white.
The film makes extensive use of colorized archival footage with reconstructed sound, which were painstakingly sourced and treated. While visually striking and effective in drawing the audience into the period, the technique can also feel a bit uncanny, making one briefly wonder whether the filmmakers had actually found such high-definition video and audio from the period.
What further humanizes the story are excerpts from several of the interviewees’ own writings about their experiences, narrated and woven into the film. It’s not a comprehensive history of Taiwan during World War II, but by focusing on individuals, it offers insight into the choices and sentiments of ordinary people swept up in the forces of history.

Taiwanese consumers grew more cautious about the economic outlook and spending this month despite the economy’s strongest growth prospects in decades, with inflation concerns and financial-market volatility weighing on sentiment, a survey released yesterday by Cathay Financial Holding Co (國泰金控) showed.
Consumer sentiment toward the local stock market and overall risk appetite fell after swings in equities last month, the survey showed.
Heightened tensions between the US and Iran, oil price gains and expectations for higher US interest rates had made investors more cautious, Cathay Financial said.
Photo: RITCHIE B. TONGO, EPA
Frequent stock trading halts in South Korea and renewed concerns about the sustainability of the artificial intelligence (AI) boom fueled market volatility, with the index measuring optimism toward Taiwanese stocks falling to 36.2 and the risk-appetite index declining to 29.1, it said.
Respondents expected inflation to average 2.3 percent this year, higher than the government’s estimate of 2.07 percent and above the central bank’s 2 percent inflation target, the survey showed.
Consumers were also less optimistic about economic growth. They expected the economy to expand 8.94 percent this year on average, well below the government’s latest forecast of 11.05 percent — the fastest pace in nearly four decades, while only about one-quarter expected growth to exceed 10 percent.
The divergence between official forecasts and household expectations suggests that the benefits of Taiwan’s AI-led expansion have yet to translate into equally strong consumer confidence, as higher energy costs, inflation risks and financial-market swings add to uncertainty, Cathay Financial said.
As a result, willingness to make major purchases weakened, with the index for durable-goods spending falling into negative territory, the survey showed.
Taiwanese equities nevertheless remained the most favored investment target over the next six months, with 57 percent of respondents selecting local equities, compared with 24 percent who favored US stocks, it found.
Among respondents planning to increase investments, the most commonly cited reason was confidence in Taiwanese companies’ ability to sustain earnings, followed by optimism about the strength of the economy, the survey said.
The survey was conducted from Aug. 1 to Aug. 7 and gathered 12,580 responses from customers and members of Cathay Life Insurance Co (國泰人壽) and Cathay United Bank Co (國泰世華銀行).

Rethinking hiring in the age of technology
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-20
16:46:29 UTC
01:46:29 KST

If a 25-year-old’s resume stands out not for a degree from a prestigious university or professional certifications, but because they have accumulated 2,000 hours playing strategy games, would Taiwan’s public sector include the applicant in its talent pool, or reject them outright?
US Secretary of Transportation Sean Duffy on Aug. 10 announced on X that the US Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) launched a program in April to recruit video game players as air traffic controllers. Within months, it had hired more than 2,000 people, achieving more than 90 percent of its annual recruitment target. What the FAA saw in these gamers-turned-air-traffic-controllers is not their gaming skills, but the abilities they developed through spending years in real-time environments with high information density.
When the government redefines experience not recognized in traditional resumes as transferable to high-risk professional work, it is changing not only how it recruits employees, but also the standards by which talent policy judges “professional competence.”
Both of my children are teachers. They spend their days dealing with students and parents, and the thing they most often do after work is play video games. For their generation, screens are part of their everyday environment — from gaming interfaces and collaborative platforms to generative artificial intelligence (AI), the cost of learning to use new tools is far lower than it was for the previous generation. That does not mean they are inherently smarter, but is a reminder that many abilities are developed outside the classroom. As AI becomes more commonplace, the digital divide would only grow wider.
Taiwan has already begun to take action. In May, the Ministry of Digital Affairs upgraded its AI talent industry accreditation guidelines to version 3.0, adding competencies in AI governance literacy and AI collaboration development. Talent cultivation is moving away from a course-and certification-centered approach toward one in which the industry defines the questions and the talent solves them.
However, the next step cannot simply be to turn these new skills into another professional certificate. The government and businesses should incorporate work samples, simulated tasks, AI collaboration tests and digital portfolios into their selection processes. What an individual has actually accomplished and what problems they are capable of solving should carry more weight than their field of study.
Talent policy should shift from offering courses by waiting for corporate recognition to define verifiable skills and designing education and training around them.
That is particularly important for the public sector. From air traffic control, cybersecurity, energy dispatch and disaster prevention to national defense, workplaces increasingly resemble information-dense human-machine collaboration systems. Safety standards cannot be relaxed, but talent recruitment pools can be broadened.
What needs to be eliminated is not academic qualifications, but a complacent system that uses them as a substitute for assessing ability.
In the AI era, the competition for talent might not be about which country teaches the most people how to use AI, but which country most quickly recognizes where skills are developed. When the next generation puts gaming experience, open-source projects, AI collaboration and simulation experience on their resumes, talent recruitment should no longer focus solely on the universities they attended or their fields of study.
Liao Ming-hui is an assistant research fellow at the Chung-Hua Institution for Economic Research.
Translated by Kyra Gustavsen
For the last 15 years, China has relied on gray zone operations to advance its territorial ambitions across Asia. And for 15 years, the US has struggled to respond. But the open door on which China has been pushing may finally be closing. Gray zone operations involve the assertive use of a variety of tools in ways that create conditions that can be described as neither peace nor war. Military forces might act provocatively — even dangerously — while carefully avoiding violence, whereas law enforcement employs nonlethal violence as a first resort. Such an approach creates difficult calculations for its targets.

Inside one of the world’s few courses in caring for ancient papyrus manuscripts
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-20
16:46:21 UTC
01:46:21 KST

Jiang Shijin pulled the precision binocular headband magnifier over her eyes and hunched down within a few inches of the ancient text resting on a light board.
Using a pair of hand tools, Jiang carefully inspected the sheet made from the papyrus plant, proceeding with the utmost care. After all, it most likely had not been handled in a century — nor read for thousands of years.
The Papyrus Conservation Summer Seminar at the University of Michigan is the only one of its kind in the Americas, the university said. It is one of the few in the world designed to convey the best practices for conserving papyrus manuscripts, ancient texts written on rolls or sheets made from the papyrus plant.
Photo: AP
Michigan’s Papyrology Collection covers texts and documents from 1000BC to 1000AD.
No institution on this side of the world has more of them, the school said, giving the researchers access to a vast collection of ancient papyri. There are portions of the Homer epics, The Odyssey and The Iliad, writings by the philosopher Epicurus and the oldest-known copy of the Epistles of Paul.
Marieka Kaye, who manages library preservation services for physical collections at the university’s library, said she tried to make “things comfortable and not scary, because a lot of people just feel terrified working on these ancient things.”
The seminar introduced the papyrologists and conservators to techniques in the treatment, storage and care of the ancient texts, as well as documentation practices.
Papyrus and its ink can crumble, smear or break, so Kaye encouraged the students to carefully remove dirt, sand, salt and debris; use controlled moisture to soften folds and realign fibers; and dry the papyrus slowly under light weight to prevent curling.
The first seminar was held in 2012, and they have been held every two years since, except for 2020. About 50 students total have taken part.
“If we don’t train the next generations of conservators, this is a craft that is going to be lost,” said Giuliano Sidro, curator of Michigan’s Papyrology Collection.
Latin professor Francis Willey Kelsey was the driving force behind the establishment of the Papyrology Collection. He believed Michigan students studying the ancient world needed access not only to books, but to the tangible remains of antiquity.
Today, the Kelsey Museum of Archaeology is a fixture on the Michigan campus. Its collection represents one of the finest compilations of daily-life objects from Greco-Roman Egypt outside of Cairo.
“This is a place where you make discoveries, potentially every day, if you just go into the vault, pick out a box and open something up, and you start reading,” Sidro said.
Of course, to make sense of it, one needs to be able to decipher Arabic, ancient Greek or Latin, and even Egyptian, one of the earliest known written languages that is now extinct. A few of the seminar participants were able to read the papyri, including Macquarie University postdoctoral fellow Arzak Mohamed, who reads Arabic, and papyrology doctoral student Mauro Castiello, who can translate ancient Greek and Latin.
Kaye said she always tries to include a student from Egypt among the seminar participants.
Mohamed, from Fayoum, Egypt, had heard about the papyrus seminar for years and always wanted to attend.
“Now, I can transfer this information from Michigan to Egypt and even in Australia,” she said. “I will be like the chain, connecting between the three countries.”
“By saving this information, we can transfer the knowledge to the next generation,” she added.

Trump cited what he said was a good relationship with North Korean leader Kim Jong-un and South Korea’s refusal to support him over the war in Iran.
On Wednesday, the South Korean and US militaries confirmed they shortened the 11-day drills by shortening their duration by about half and canceling some field training exercises. The reduction of the exercises raised worries about the allies’ joint defense posture.
Kim Yo-jong, the sister of North Korea’s leader, dismissed Trump’s overture, saying: “The provocative, aggressive nature of the drills won’t change even though their duration and size were reduced.”
“If the US calculates that it can propagate its recent measure as the one of so-called good faith, they will not get the desired answer,” she said.
She denied Trump’s claim that Kim Jong-un had responded to his request for a conversation, but said personal relations between her brother and Trump are “still excellent.” That signals North Korea would want to wait for Trump to make bigger concessions before returning to talks.
Asked by reporters if he would be meeting with Kim Jong-un this year, Trump said: “Yeah, I will be.”
The Ulchi Freedom Shield is one of the main military exercises conducted by the US and South Korea annually to enhance their ability to cope with potential North Korean aggression.
Washington and Seoul say their drills are defensive in nature, but Pyongyang calls them an invasion rehearsal and often reacts with weapons tests.
Meanwhile, South Korea sought China’s support in reviving talks with North Korea.
South Korean Minister of Foreign Affairs Cho Hyun called for China to play a constructive role in facilitating North Korea’s swift return to dialogue during a meeting with his Chinese counterpart, Wang Yi (王毅), in Seoul.
Asked whether Beijing might help mediate a summit between Trump and Kim, Wang said it is a matter for the two sides to decide.
Wang also urged South Korea not to take sides between Beijing and Washington.
“The fundamental solution to the tensions on the Korean Peninsula lies in addressing the root causes of the problem and urging the United States to abandon its hostile policy toward North Korea,” the Xinhua news agency cited Wang as saying.
China hopes South Korea will “achieve genuine strategic autonomy, refrain from bloc confrontation and taking sides, and develop relations with major powers including China and the United States in parallel and without contradiction,” he said.
“China would be glad to see the peninsula move toward peaceful coexistence between South Korea and North Korea,” Wang said, calling for a restart of dialogue and restoration of trust.
He urged Seoul to adhere to a friendly policy toward China, saying bilateral ties had “fully recovered” and made positive progress this year.
“A rational, pragmatic, and positive policy towards China is entirely in line with South Korea’s interests and the trend of the times,” he said.
Wang also called for an early completion of second-stage talks with South Korea for a free trade agreement, saying the two countries should promote regional economic integration amid intensifying fragmentation in the global economy and rising trade protectionism, Xinhua reported.

70% in Taiwan view Chinese coast guard patrols as ‘ill will’: MAC poll
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-20
16:46:20 UTC
01:46:20 KST

Seven in 10 people in Taiwan view recent Chinese coast guard patrols in waters east of Taiwan as an act of “ill will,” according to a Mainland Affairs Council (MAC) poll released Thursday.
The survey found that 70.5 percent of respondents regarded the patrols as malicious, while 7.5 percent considered them an act of goodwill and 22 percent had no opinion.
The question was included amid a series of operations by Chinese coast guard, other government and research vessels in waters east of Taiwan since June, including what Beijing has described as “special maritime law-enforcement operations.”
Photo: Taipei Times
Taiwan authorities have accused Beijing of using such operations to create the “false impression” that it has jurisdiction over the area, while China has maintained that its maritime law-enforcement activities are lawful and aimed at safeguarding what it considers its territorial sovereignty and maritime rights.
Meanwhile, 76.4 percent supported amending the law to impose heavier penalties on people from overseas who commit violent crimes in Taiwan, following a July incident in which a Hong Kong man attacked media commentator Akio Yaita in Taichung, the poll showed.
Eleven percent opposed such a move, while 12.5 percent expressed no opinion.
The incident has drawn concern in Taiwan over possible Chinese transnational repression, with the Taiwanese government saying it is considering heavier penalties for actions commissioned, directed, or funded by hostile foreign forces.
The poll also found broad opposition to Beijing’s political proposals for Taiwan, with 81.2 percent saying they opposed the “one country, two systems” formula, under which Taiwan would be treated as a special administrative region under Chinese Communist Party (CCP) rule.
Meanwhile, 83.6 percent favored broadly maintaining the status quo, while 83.9 percent supported the position that Taiwan’s future should be decided by its 23 million people.
The three issues are long-running questions in the MAC’s surveys, with the latest results broadly in line with previous polls and showing a largely stable trend over time.
In a separate question, 68.9 percent agreed that “Taiwan should maintain the status quo and reject unification with the CCP,” while 18.3 percent disagreed.
Asked which consideration was more important in cross- strait exchanges, 46.9 percent chose safeguarding national sovereignty, slightly higher than the 40.9 percent who chose promoting economic development.
The survey, commissioned by MAC, was conducted by National Chengchi University’s Election Study Center from Aug. 13-17 via telephone interviews with adults aged 20 and above in Taiwan.
According to MAC, 1,086 valid responses were collected, with a confidence level of 95 percent and a margin of error of plus or minus 2.97 percentage points.

Finance ministry to announce tax lottery winners
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-20
16:46:18 UTC
01:46:18 KST

The winners of a lottery for taxpayers, including foreign nationals, who filed last year’s individual income tax returns using a mobile device are to be announced at 4pm today, the Ministry of Finance said on Wednesday.
Prizes include cash awards of up to NT$50,000 and electronic vouchers worth NT$200 or NT$500; winners must claim them by Nov. 25, the ministry said.
The winners are to be announced on the ministry’s Facebook page and the Web sites of regional taxation bureaus.
Photo: Lo Pei-de, Taipei Times
According to the National Taxation Bureau, 2.89 million individual income tax returns were filed using mobile devices this year, an increase of more than 290,000, or 11.15 percent, from the previous year.
Among more than 2.64 million eligible households, 19,586 are to receive prizes, including 86 cash prizes and 19,500 digital coupon prizes, the bureau said.
The cash prizes consist of one NT$50,000 top prize, five NT$20,000 prizes, 10 NT$10,000 prizes, 20 NT$5,000 prizes and 50 NT$2,000 prizes.
The digital prizes include 3,000 NT$500 electronic vouchers and 16,500 NT$200 electronic vouchers.
Cash prize winners would be notified by registered mail, and the prize money is to be deposited directly into their designated bank accounts, the bureau said.
Winners of electronic coupons are to receive a text message with the sender ID “111,” indicating that the message is an official government message.
The message would be sent to phone numbers registered with the tax filing system and would include a link to the ministry’s Web site with instructions on how to redeem the prize, it added.
Under tax regulations, cash prizes exceeding NT$20,000 are subject to a 10 percent withholding tax, which would be deducted automatically.
The bureau said it would never notify winners by phone or ask them to use an ATM to claim their prizes.
It also would never require winners to pay taxes in advance and urged people to remain vigilant against lottery scams.

Fidelity International plans to pull out of wholly owned China fund unit, sources say
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-20
16:46:17 UTC
01:46:17 KST

Fidelity International (FIL) plans to exit its wholly owned China fund unit, two people familiar with the matter said, marking one of the biggest retreats by a global asset manager from the world’s second-largest economy.
London-headquartered FIL, which manages US$1.18 trillion in client assets globally, is weighing a total retreat from its onshore fund unit three years after its launch, according to the two people who spoke on condition of anonymity because the exit plan is not public.
A combination of fierce local competition, frequent leadership turnover and chronic struggles to build scale ultimately convinced global FIL executives that the China retail venture was untenable, the people said.
Photo: Reuters
The planned departure highlights the growing headwinds for foreign financial firms in China, with squeezed margins hampering expansion since Beijing allowed fully foreign-owned units in 2020, attracting six global asset managers to set up new onshore operations including Fidelity and BlackRock Inc.
“China remains an important market for Fidelity International and we continue to believe it offers attractive long-term opportunities both for our business and for investors. There is no change to report on our strategy or market presence,” FIL told Reuters in a statement.
Boston-based Fidelity Investments originally set up FIL as its international unit, before spinning it off as an independent business in 1980. Both FIL and Fidelity Investments are chaired by American businesswoman Abigail Johnson.
It remains unclear how FIL plans to restructure or liquidate its 14 China retail fund products, which hold 4.5 billion yuan (US$670 million) in assets. That’s well below a target set for 2029, according to a 2024 internal document reviewed by Reuters. The firm believed then that the China fund unit needed at least US$14 billion in assets to be profitable.
FIL assets under management peaked one year after the unit’s launch at 6 billion yuan, before dropping 25 percent from there as of the end of June, the latest reports on its China products showed.
The Shanghai-based unit employs nearly 100 people, according to one of the sources.
The China Securities Regulatory Commission told Reuters it has not received any official withdrawal application from FIL.
Any FIL plan to exit its China fund unit would be subject to change and require regulatory approval. The planned exit would, however, represent one of the most prominent retrenchments from China’s US$5.9 trillion public fund market by a foreign asset manager over the last decade.
FIL has so far put US$218 million into the unit, the largest among all foreign wholly owned fund houses, topping BlackRock’s US$215 million, business registration records showed.
Just last month, British rival Schroders PLC became the first foreign manager to exit its wholly owned onshore fund unit — which managed US$250 million in local assets — offloading its products to Neuberger Berman Group LLC amid scaling struggles, according to announcements from both firms.
The Schroders move followed earlier pullbacks by other peers, including Legal & General Group PLC, which halted its China expansion plans, and Vanguard Group Inc, which closed its local fund sales joint venture and abandoned plans to enter the mutual fund sector.
Any FIL exit from China’s onshore mutual fund market would cap a broader, gradual pullback in China, an economy which lost momentum at the start of the second half of this year on weaker industrial output and consumption.
FIL cut about 500 positions at its Dalian technology and operations center in late 2024 over data concerns, having already cut 16 percent of the local fund management staff earlier that year amid sluggish growth and cost pressures.
The China fund management business has experienced rapid leadership churn since its inception five years ago, cycling through four board chairmen and three chief executives.

8 gym dos and don’ts from fitness experts
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-20
16:46:16 UTC
01:46:16 KST

I like to think of myself as a fairly laid-back person. Other people’s behavior is not my business. There is one notable exception: my gym nemesis.
He brings his computer to the gym and takes work conference calls at full volume. He has four to six pairs of dumbbells around him at all times — then doesn’t put them away. Intellectually I understand he is a fragile, flawed human like the rest of us, but in my gut I sometimes wonder if he arrived here from another galaxy.
Life is full of unspoken rules, and the gym is no different. The heavy weights, sweaty people and mysterious machines can make it daunting to figure out how to behave. So we asked fitness experts for their thoughts on gym etiquette — their biggest pet peeves as well as the behaviors that might seem intimidating, but are actually fine.
Photo: Reuters
Good gym etiquette is less about following a long list of rules than it is simple respect, says Mathew Forzaglia, a fitness professional and educator. “Respect the equipment, respect other people’s time and space, and respect the shared environment,” he says.
GYM DON’TS
DON’T LEAVE A MESS
Whether it’s leaving a bench covered in your sweat, or not re-racking weights after you use them, failing to clean and reset equipment after you use it is not only a hygiene issue, it’s potentially unsafe.
Leaving out heavy plates or dumbbells “creates an accessibility issue for people who physically can’t move the weight someone else abandoned,” says Amanda Katz, a New York City-based personal trainer and run coach.
As for wiping off your sweat, “it’s common courtesy and takes just a few seconds,” Forzaglia says. “No one wants to lie down on a bench covered in someone else’s sweat.”
DON’T HOARD EQUIPMENT
If you’re planning to do a complex circuit training routine that involves having access to six machines at once, save it for a home workout or tweak it to be more sequential.
“You can’t claim the cable machine and the leg press and three sets of dumbbells,” says Laura Girard, certified personal trainer, strength coach and founder of The Energy Academy in New York City. “Learn to share.”
DON’T OFFER UNSOLICITED ADVICE
It can feel intoxicating to think you know better than others. Spot someone across the gym doing deadlifts with what you think is bad form, and it might be tempting to go over and give them a few tips. Don’t.
“Unless someone is in immediate danger, I don’t think it’s appropriate to offer coaching to strangers,” Katz says. Most of us are not fitness professionals, and even if we are, we don’t know why someone might be training the way they are.
“There are countless reasons an exercise might look different than expected — from injury rehabilitation to a coach’s programming,” Katz says.
Other people’s bodies and how they train them are not your business. “Never assume you know somebody’s goals or body better than they do,” Girard says.
DON’T BE LOUD
Whether it’s playing your pump-up playlist sans headphones, grunting loudly through exercises — or, as I encountered in my gym just the other week, a man shouting “LET’S GO!” before every set of shoulder shrugs — being loud is not fair or pleasant for your fellow gym-goer.
“Everyone deserves their own playlist and to not have their nervous system frayed by a random shout when they’re already doing something vulnerable and uncomfortable,” Girard says.
PHONE ETIQUETTE
Resting between sets is normal and fine — more on this later. But monopolizing a machine because you’re scrolling social media, answering e-mails or taking calls is not.
“The gym is for training,” Forzaglia says. “If you need to catch up on your phone, step outside for a minute.”
Don’t show up late to a group class
“I understand that life happens and sometimes you’re running late,” says Jessie Diaz-Herrera, co-founder and fitness instructor at Power Plus Wellness in New York City. But walking into a class 15 or 20 minutes late can be extremely disruptive to other participants, and potentially present a safety issue “if the instructor has already gone through the warm-up or explained the movements”, she says.
GYM OKAYS
DO TALK TO PEOPLE
While unsolicited advice is never welcome, this doesn’t mean you have to completely ignore other people at the gym.
“Most people at the gym are either also new, or love the gym and would be happy to chat your ear off,” Girard says.
As long as you don’t interrupt someone in the middle of a set, Girard says it’s “totally OK to approach for a quick form check or help with equipment.” (But wait for a go-ahead or an invitation from them to strike up a longer conversation.)
It’s also fine to politely ask someone how many sets they have left, or if you can work in between their sets, Forzaglia says.
“Most experienced gym-goers appreciate respectful communication,” he says. “I’d much rather someone ask than stand around waiting or skip an exercise because they felt uncomfortable speaking up.”
DO REST BETWEEN SETS
Although you shouldn’t disappear into your phone for long stretches, resting on or around equipment for a minute or two between sets of exercise is normal and expected.
“Rest is part of strength training and Hiit protocols, and most people understand that,” Katz says. “You don’t need to rush through your workout to look like you belong or keep your heart rate up unless it’s the intention of the session.”
DO RECORD YOURSELF
Recording your workout is not inherently rude, Diaz-Herrera says. “A lot of people use videos to check their form, track their progress or create content,” she says.
The important thing is to not intentionally film others.
If you think you might be in someone’s video and don’t want to be, Diaz-Herrera says it’s absolutely OK to ask whether you appear in frame, and if they mind moving the camera or cropping you out.
“That’s not being difficult or making a big deal out of it,” she says. “It’s just communicating and respecting each other’s space.”

01:46:16 KST

The Executive Yuan yesterday budgeted for a provisional increase of nearly 6 percent in pensions for public-sector retirees, adding NT$11.4 billion (US$357.1 million) to planned government spending.
Pensions for retired government workers are provisionally budgeted to increase by 5.89 percent to keep up with inflation, based on the cumulative consumer price index as of May, an Executive Yuan spokesperson told a news conference after a Cabinet meeting.
The central government is to contribute NT$7.4 billion and local governments are to contribute NT$4 billion to cover the cost of the increase, officials said.
Photo: Liu Hsin-de, Taipei Times
Although the increase is more than the 4 percent pay raise planned for public-sector workers, the Cabinet said it would adjust benefits and increase professional and supervisory-position allowances by NT$2,000, in addition to the pay raise.
That would result in a cumulative 5.88 to 9.98 percent pay raise for nonsupervisory civil servants and a 6.39 percent to 11.56 percent cumulative raise for supervisors, it said.
A Directorate-General of Personnel Administration spokesperson said military service members are included in the pay increases and would receive other allowances depending on their occupational specialty.
The Executive Yuan in February approved making personnel in qualifying drone units eligible for the combat unit allowance, they said.
Combat unit allowance eligibility was broadened to include personnel in operational-sustainment units at or below brigade level, they said.
The scheme would allow conscripts in combat units to receive the same combat unit allowances as volunteers serving in the same roles, they said.
It would increase the monthly salary of a private second class to NT$57,330 and a battalion commander holding the rank of lieutenant colonel to NT$100,360, up 48.43 percent and 33.12 percent respectively, they said.
Dangerous-duty allowance supplements for police officers and firefighters, which vary by locality, could reach a maximum additional 130 percent of the underlying allowance in Taipei and New Taipei City, while the criminal-work supplement for qualifying police officers would also increase, the spokesperson said.
The measure would benefit about 81,000 police officers and firefighters, they said.
Eligibility for performance-based bonuses and bonuses for dangerous or nighttime duties would also be broadened, they added.
During their review of the budget, opposition lawmakers had demanded a NT$30,000 monthly allowance for volunteer military personnel and a higher income replacement rate for police officers and firefighters.
As the measures were excluded from the budget, lawmakers yesterday led retired police officers and firefighters in a protest outside the Executive Yuan in Taipei.
Premier Cho Jung-tai (卓榮泰) said that the income replacement rate for a police officer with 35 years of service could already reach 69 percent.
Efforts to improve public-sector compensation are ongoing, he said, adding that salaries have been raised four times over the past decade, with a fifth raise planned for next year, and multiple allowances have been adjusted since last year.

In cutting joint drills, Trump has given South Korea’s president what he wants. So why is Seoul so uneasy?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-20
16:46:15 UTC
01:46:15 KST

At their first summit in August last year South Korean President Lee Jae-myung, told US President Donald Trump: “If you, Mr President, become the peacemaker, then I will assist you as the pacemaker.”
The remark at the Oval Office captured the thrust of Lee’s approach to North Korea: Dial down the military posturing and make repeated peace overtures to revive dialogue, even if they have been consistently rejected by Pyongyang largely over Seoul’s insistence on denuclearization.
Fast forward to this week, and Trump’s move to cut joint military exercises with South Korea echoes what Lee had himself floated, on several occasions, as a possible tool for drawing Pyongyang back to the table.
Illustration: Mountain People
Lee’s broader message is that South Korea should take more responsibility for its own defense and reduce its reliance on others. On Tuesday, he used the moment to renew calls for wartime operational control of the military and progress on his country’s nuclear submarine program.
Trump has delivered on the drills, albeit in the blunt, discourteous fashion typical of the president: via social media, hours before the drills were to begin.
Yet the move has inverted South Korea’s usual political lines, where the left-right divide is shaped more by attitudes toward North Korea — hawks vs doves, confrontation vs engagement — than by economic or social values.
Reducing joint drills has long been advocated by some on the South Korean left. A right-wing US president imposing the policy on his center-left South Korean counterpart lands awkwardly for both sides.
While some see the reduction as potentially useful for diplomacy, the louder concern in Seoul is that Trump is weakening a key pillar of deterrence and leaving South Korea with little say over decisions that directly affect its security. That might strain an alliance that has been the bedrock of security on the peninsula since the Korean War.
The opposition conservative People Power Party has called the decision a “security disaster” and warned of a return to “Korea passing,” a term used when Seoul feels sidelined in matters directly affecting it. Conservative newspapers have been almost unanimous in calling the cut reckless. The influential Chosun Ilbo has gone further, blaming Lee’s government directly for inviting it.
The left has not shared that sense of alarm. The Hankyoreh, one of the country’s main progressive papers, raised no objection to the substance of Trump’s decision, only to how it was delivered: unilaterally and disrespectfully on social media, calling it “regrettable.” The Kyunghyang Shinmun took a more positive view, saying the cut could help create an atmosphere for dialogue with North Korea, so long as deterrence held.
Reducing tensions with North Korea and creating space for dialogue are central to Lee’s agenda. The ruling party has been quiet on the move, but openly welcoming Trump’s decision could put it at odds with a base that has viewed Trump with suspicion, if not hostility.
Aside from domestic politics, the episode is likely to deepen doubts about Washington’s commitment to its allies, doubts that have been building for years since Trump’s first term, Sogang University international relations professor Kim Jaechun said.
Trust, he argued, is the foundation of any alliance, and remarks like Trump’s reinforce the impression that the US’ obligations are increasingly viewed “through a highly transactional lens,” one that could shape how South Koreans judge US reliability long after Trump has left office.
Then there is the issue of the nuclear deterrent. South Korea enjoys protection under the US nuclear umbrella, but public support for an independent deterrent among South Koreans and their neighbors has hovered at about 70 percent or more in surveys. The latest news might push that support higher still.
Kim said he expects Pyongyang to welcome any sign of friction within the alliance, but doubts that it views improving relations with Washington as a priority, given the stronger backing it now enjoys from China and Russia compared with during Trump’s first term.
“The irony is that [US] policies intended to reduce American burdens may ultimately strengthen calls for independent nuclear deterrents among US allies,” he said.
For the last 15 years, China has relied on gray zone operations to advance its territorial ambitions across Asia. And for 15 years, the US has struggled to respond. But the open door on which China has been pushing may finally be closing. Gray zone operations involve the assertive use of a variety of tools in ways that create conditions that can be described as neither peace nor war. Military forces might act provocatively — even dangerously — while carefully avoiding violence, whereas law enforcement employs nonlethal violence as a first resort. Such an approach creates difficult calculations for its targets.

Unknown
Unknown Publisher

16:46:14 UTC
01:46:14 KST

China Steel Corp (CSC, 中鋼), the nation’s biggest steelmaker, yesterday reported a 55 percent month-on-month slump in pretax profit for last month, as sliding steel demand in Asia drove lower gross profit.
Pretax profit dipped to NT$655 million (US$20.52 million) from a 47-month high of NT$1.47 billion in June, snapping three consecutive months of growth, the company said in a statement.
Operating profit plummeted 84 percent month-on-month to NT$241 million from NT$1.52 billion, it said.
Photo: CNA
In the first seven months of the year, cumulative pretax profit improved to NT$2.99 billion, reversing a pretax loss of NT$2.41 billion in the corresponding period last year, while operating profit rose to NT$3.29 billion from a loss of NT$2.27 billion a year earlier, the company said.
Over the same period, revenue rose 3 percent to NT$197.72 billion from NT$192.66 billion, and shipments increased 2 percent to 4.45 million tonnes from 4.36 million tonnes, it said.
While steel prices in the US and Europe remain firm amid trade protection policies curbing steel imports, prices in Asia are declining due to overcapacity, the Kaohsiung-based company said.
However, an easing drop in steel prices in Vietnam after Chinese steelmakers cut production to improve profitability, and lower inventories in the Taiwanese supply chain, show an early sign that the slump in Asia is near the bottom, the company said.
Challenges remain as the ongoing Middle East conflict drives crude oil prices higher and adds more pressure to steelmakers’ manufacturing costs, it said.

Fifteen are indicted for evading military service
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-20
16:46:14 UTC
01:46:14 KST

The New Taipei City Prosecutors’ Office on Wednesday indicted 15 people for evading mandatory military service or assisting others in doing so, including a former boy band member and a rapper.
Prosecutors uncovered the scheme last year following an investigation into actor Darren Wang (王大陸), who allegedly faked a heart condition to avoid mandatory military service with the assistance of Chen Chi-ming (陳志明).
In April, Wang was sentenced to six months in prison for unlawfully obtaining personal data to avoid service.
Photo: Taipei Times
The office on Wednesday indicted 15 people, including Chen, Chiu Sheng-yi (邱勝翊, better known as Prince, 王子) from the Taiwanese boy band Lollipop, rapper Chang Jie-rui (張傑瑞) and Internet personality Shao Kai-hung (邵凱宏).
The charges included forgery and evading conscription by illegally manipulating one’s physical status.
According to the indictment, Chen was exempt from military service due to severe hypertension.
Beginning in 2011, Chen charged 12 conscripts between NT$50,000 and NT$350,000 each, and told them to hold their breath to artificially raise their blood pressure readings, prosecutors said.
Chen would then wear a blood pressure monitor at their residence to help them obtain medical certificates showing severe hypertension, they said.
Chiu admitted during questioning that he did not have hypertension and had paid Chen NT$300,000 to help him evade service, prosecutors said.
By the time investigators launched the first three crackdowns, several other members of Lollipop had already been implicated, they said.
Chiu nevertheless did not voluntarily turn himself in, and instead repeatedly denied the allegations, they added.
Given Chiu’s statutory one-year service term, prosecutors recommended that he be sentenced to at least two years and two months in prison.
Prosecutors recommended the same sentence for four other conscripts whose statutory service term was one year.
For five others who were required to serve four months, prosecutors are seeking sentences of at least one year.
As two other conscripts denied the charges, prosecutors are recommending sentences of at least one year and three months and one year and six months respectively.
Prosecutors recommended that Chen Chih-ming, whom they described as having played a key role in the scheme, be sentenced to at least five years in prison.
“If they receive probation or are allowed to commute a fine, it would send a message to all other conscripts that ... even if they get caught, the problem can be easily solved through money,” the office said, recommending that the court not grant leniency.
