EDITORIAL: AI cyberattack highlights risk
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-20
16:46:11 UTC
01:46:11 KST

In a hacking campaign last month believed to be linked to China, artificial intelligence (AI) agents launched 12 waves of attacks against the government in four days, which is believed to be the first disclosed case of a fully AI autonomous attack against a government.
The Financial Times on Wednesday last week reported that researchers at Dream Security, an Israeli AI company, were the first to detect the intrusion. Dream Security showed that the attackers used open-source AI agents, such as OpenClaw, to build an autonomous hacking tool that coordinated the cyberintrusion, describing it as “a first-of-its-kind breach.”
Researchers said that internal communications linked to the cyberattack were in simplified Chinese, suggesting the operators were likely connected to China.
Taiwan is no stranger to China’s “hybrid warfare,” from military drills and disinformation campaigns to escalating cyberattacks. According to the National Security Bureau, Taiwan’s critical infrastructure and government networks faced an average of 2.6 million cyberbreaches per day from China last year, a 6 percent increase from 2024.
However, last month’s AI-driven cyberintrusion was an advanced tactic, involving a hybrid approach combining manual operations and conventional hacking with AI agents. AI might become the main player in cyberattacks, moving beyond simply assisting human hackers.
The reports have triggered deep concern domestically and internationally.
The Ministry of Digital Affairs said in a statement that its Administration for Cybersecurity detected last month’s cyberattack, which it said originated overseas, and immediately launched an investigation. The ministry warned that AI agents could rapidly integrate multiple attack techniques.
The threat of AI-assisted hacking has escalated dramatically with international AI labs releasing more advanced models that can rapidly conduct reconnaissance, identify vulnerabilities and take advantage of their findings.
Numerous reports have documented cases of advanced AI models conducting unauthorized actions without human intervention, raising fears of the proliferation of AI-enabled cyberattacks. OpenAI and Anthropic reported that their new models have escaped test environments and hacked into other systems.
The cyberattack on Taiwan has demonstrated how autonomous AI agents could change the nature of cyberwarfare. If AI with autonomous decisionmaking capabilities were weaponized by malicious nations or criminal groups, all individuals, corporations, critical networks and infrastructure, or even entire countries, would be targets. It could also significantly reduce the cost of attacks, while the effort to defend against them becomes more difficult.
Taiwan faces a challenge that Western democracies also have to confront. Dream Security chief strategy officer Amir Becker, a former head of the Israel Defense Forces’ cyberoperations and signals intelligence division, said that the advent of AI tools means governments must assume that they face a permanent cyberattack.
The spread of autonomous AI systems has raised pressing questions about legislative responses, technical protections and the ability of governments to respond to threats.
President William Lai (賴清德) has vowed to make Taiwan a “Smart Nation 2.0,” with plans to invest more than NT$1.5 trillion (US$46.99 billion) by 2040 in the “Ten New AI infrastructure Projects.”
Besides promoting the AI economy, Taiwan urgently needs to upgrade its cyberdefense strategy to safeguard digital sovereignty, which is crucial to national sovereignty.
In addition to improving information systems, a robust national digital defense is needed, meaning that legislation and technical capabilities need to be enhanced. That includes the digital resilience of critical infrastructure and networks, advanced surveillance to oversee system vulnerabilities and operational risks, multiple lines of defense to block attacks in a timely manner, and backup systems to ensure operational sustainability.
Cybersecurity cannot be a matter of “each taking care of their own business.” Governments, businesses and the cybersecurity community must work together to improve defensive resilience to minimize the damage from attacks.
Taiwan also needs to deepen cooperation with like-minded countries to establish a cross-border real-time AI security intelligence-sharing mechanism, partnering with international AI security organizations to enhance algorithmic defenses and combat cyberattackers’ supply chains.
If a country cannot protect its digital sovereignty, it might lose its national autonomy. Taiwan must be prepared in every aspect of national defense.
For the last 15 years, China has relied on gray zone operations to advance its territorial ambitions across Asia. And for 15 years, the US has struggled to respond. But the open door on which China has been pushing may finally be closing. Gray zone operations involve the assertive use of a variety of tools in ways that create conditions that can be described as neither peace nor war. Military forces might act provocatively — even dangerously — while carefully avoiding violence, whereas law enforcement employs nonlethal violence as a first resort. Such an approach creates difficult calculations for its targets.

16:46:10 UTC

England’s Ollie Robinson and Josh Tongue shared both the wickets and the match ball as they joined forces to bowl out Pakistan on the opening day of the first Test at Headingley on Wednesday.
The two paceman took five wickets each as Pakistan were dismissed for a meager 171 on the first day of England’s post-Bazball era, with Joe Root starting his second stint as full-time England captain following the shock international retirement of former skipper Ben Stokes.
Root rounded off a fine day on his Yorkshire home ground reaching 37 not out at stumps, with England 112-2 — a deficit of just 59 runs.
Photo: Reuters
Robinson took a wicket with the very first ball of the match and dismissed four top-order batsmen in a haul of 5-51.
Tongue followed up the Sussex seamer’s initial burst with 5-46.
Normally when a bowler takes five wickets in a Test innings, he keeps the ball as a souvenir.
However, with Robinson and Tongue performing the feat on Wednesday they asked a member of the groundstaff to saw it in half. Robinson, showing off the newly sliced ball at his post-match press conference, told reporters: “As we were walking off Tonguey said: ‘I think we should split it.’”
“I was like, ‘yeah, we should actually do that, I think it’d be quite cool,’” he said.
“I said ‘do you reckon they’ll be able to do it?’ and within five minutes they brought it back up and it was done. It’s one of those things that you don’t really have too many halves of... half a cricket ball. It’s something we’ll never forget really and it’s not too often two guys get five in the same innings, so it’s a nice gesture and something to remember,” he added.
Robinson took a career-best seven wickets in an innings during England’s first Test of their home season, against New Zealand in June. That was his first appearance for England in more than two-and-a-half years, with team management long concerned about Robinson’s fitness rather than his skill.
Robinson, who recently became a father for the second time, added: “We had the newborn last Thursday at 2:00am so I’ve been catching up on my sleep since I got to the hotel in Leeds. But it was a really special week last week having another baby and it almost makes today even sweeter.”

01:46:10 KST

The Cabinet yesterday approved the central government’s budget proposal for next year, which would allocate NT$1.1225 trillion (US$35.16 billion) for defense, or 3.01 percent of projected GDP.
President William Lai (賴清德) has set a goal of keeping Taiwan’s defense budget above 3 percent of GDP while gradually increasing the share to 5 percent by 2030.
The defense spending plan — an 18 percent increase from this year — includes NT$691.9 billion in the Ministry of National Defense budget, NT$218.2 billion in special budgets and NT$60.7 billion in nonprofit special funds, the Directorate-General of Budget, Accounting and Statistics (DGBAS) said.
Photo: Liu Hsin-de, Taipei Times
Comptroller Bureau head Hsieh Chi-hsien (謝其賢) said the ministry’s plans include supplementary spending on drones and missiles, for which the government had previously been unable to obtain legislative approval.
The defense budget also includes NT$103.8 billion for military pensions and NT$47.9 billion for the Coast Guard Administration, the DGBAS said, adding that the calculation mirrors the method used by NATO, on which Lai has modeled Taiwan’s defense budget planning.
The overall defense budget would account for 3.01 percent of GDP, based on DGBAS’ forecast this month that GDP would be NT$37.3 trillion.
The figure represents a decline as a share of GDP from this year’s defense budget, which accounts for 3.32 percent of GDP.
The proposed budget totals NT$3.9266 trillion, up NT$891.6 billion, or 29.4 percent, from NT$3.035 trillion for this year, the DGBAS said.
The government estimates that revenue next year would be NT$3.9266 trillion, an increase of NT$1.0643 trillion, or 37.2 percent, from NT$2.8623 trillion this year.
At NT$1.1889 trillion, social welfare spending would rise 41.1 percent from this year, the DGBAS said.
The government plans to allocate NT$373 billion for population-related policies, including NT$329.5 billion for its family support program, which includes monthly cash handouts of NT$5,000 for children up to age 18.
As for technology, NT$229.2 billion has been earmarked for technological development programs, including NT$40.8 billion for artificial intelligence-related programs.
The budget also includes NT$235.7 billion for NT$10,000 cash handouts for all Taiwanese, and NT$39.2 billion for salary increases for military personnel, civil servants and public-school teachers.
Funds to support small and medium-sized enterprises would rise from NT$14.8 billion last year to NT$22.2 billion.
The proposed budget would be balanced between revenue and expenditure, with NT$179 billion in borrowing needed to finance debt repayments.
The DGBAS projected that outstanding debt at the end of next year would be NT$6.8831 trillion, equivalent to 23.4 percent of the average nominal GDP of the preceding three years and below the 40.6 percent ceiling for debt with a maturity of one year or longer.
The Cabinet is expected to submit the budget to the Legislative Yuan for review by the end of this month.
The opposition-dominated legislature only passed this year’s budget late on Friday last week after months of delays.
Additional reporting by Hollie Younger and Reuters

‘Chainsmoker Cat’ anime draws parental concern
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-20
16:46:08 UTC
01:46:08 KST

Chainsmoker Cat (尼古喵喵), an anime show, might contravene the Tobacco Hazards Prevention Act (菸害防制法) by promoting smoking, the John Tung Foundation said yesterday, adding that it has submitted a formal complaint.
Lin Ching-li (林清麗), head of the foundation’s tobacco hazard prevention center, said that it received complaints from parents that the entire show was about smoking.
While it does show the benefits of quitting, from about 3 minutes, 56 seconds into the first episode, multiple tobacco brands are given intentional closeups, Lin said.
Photo: CNA
The show depicts the main character, a cat person named Yaniko, taking several cigarettes from a box to make room for a lighter, Lin said, adding that such scenes attempt to highlight and promote tobacco brands and establish the image that smoking is good.
Lo Su-ying (羅素英), head of the Health Promotion Administration’s Tobacco Control Division, said that images from the anime published by media platforms might be in contravention of Article 12 of the act.
The agency has asked local health departments to investigate the issue, Lo said, adding that if the accusations are shown to be true, the media platforms could be fined a maximum of NT$1 million (US$31,323).
Former Consumers’ Foundation chairman You Kai-hsiung (游開雄) said that Article 12 specifically bans the promotion of tobacco products through television, movies, recordings, the Internet and other methods.
The digital age has increased the avenues to promote products, You said, adding that the authorities should not allow entertainment to be a protective umbrella for tobacco promotion.
Action Alliance on Basic Education president Wang Han-yang (王瀚陽) said that the Hong Kong Department of Health has banned the series on the grounds that it contravened Hong Kong’s Smoking (Public Health) Ordinance.
Inaction by Taiwan’s government might send the wrong message that Taiwan allows tobacco products to be promoted as long as they are packaged in entertainment content, Wang said.

Reforestation saw 5,339 trees planted at site in Pingtung
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-20
16:46:07 UTC
01:46:07 KST

Reforestation by the Taiwan Forestry Research Institute in Pingtung County’s Hengchun Township (恆春) has resulted in the planting of 5,339 trees of 18 native species over the past three-plus years.
The institute was commissioned by the Pingtung Ocean and Fisheries Affairs Management Office to reforest 2.64 hectares in a coastal area near Oluanpi (鵝鑾鼻).
The county government has been expanding Singhai Fishing Harbor (興海漁港) since 2021, with the project involving the deregistration of protected forest, requiring the developer to compensate vegetation cover.
Photo courtesy of the Taiwan Forestry Research Institute via CNA
The institute removed invasive plant species and planted 5,339 trees of 18 indigenous species — including Indian almond, Alexandrian laurel, coast hibiscus, lantern tree, screw pine, five-stamens China laurel, Obovata planchonella, common Cerberus and Formosan date palm — across about 0.7 hectares on the reforestation land, it said.
The institute interlaced seeds with seed-grown plants to accelerate the formation of vegetation cover and forest structures, it said.
The method has the potential to be applied to coastal forest restoration in other areas of southern Taiwan, it added.
In 2023, the land was covered with invasive plants, such as white popinac, siam weed and giant sensitive plant, the institute said.
However, the reforestation efforts have resulted in native trees growing to more than 1.6m tall and the development of a multilayered forest structure, it said, adding that there are also naturally regenerated seedlings growing.
Researchers observed wildlife in the restored forest, including Formosan hares, yellow-gray freshwater crabs, Taiwan bulbuls, skinks and tree lizards, showing that the forest ecosystems are recovering and that planting native species can benefit ecological restoration, the institute said.
While the site is exposed to strong northeast monsoon winds and is in a sika deer foraging hotspot, soil and irrigation improvement work and deer-proof fencing would help the seedlings survive, it said.
The survival rate of the reforested trees at the site was 1.65 times the standard after three years, showing that proper reforestation approaches can improve habitat quality and boost biodiversity, it said.
The reforestation work proves that environmental development and ecological compensation must go hand in hand, it added.

The power of Virgo’s gentle recalibration
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-20
16:46:05 UTC
01:46:05 KST

In a past Golden Age, Astraea, the Goddess of Justice, was the last deity to leave the human world. As the world descended from purity into the Iron Age of greed and falsehood, she did everything in her power to turn the tide, striving to guide all that had gone astray back onto the right path. Even after she ascended into the night sky and became the constellation Virgo, that power of “recalibrating imbalance” never disappeared.
Every year, from August 23 to September 22, the energy of Virgo becomes increasingly clear. This energy is not about finding fault, nor is it about returning to some rigid idea of “perfection.” Rather, it helps us notice the subtle ways in which we may be drifting away from what is true to ourselves, allowing us to see where adjustments can be made and where new opportunities may lie. The seeds that have taken root and grown over the past six months are now approaching their first harvest. Through this initial harvest, we are given the opportunity to examine the causes and effects that have deviated from their original intentions, and to make more precise adjustments before the next round of sowing.
This month is an especially good time to look for the areas of life that need recalibration. Virgo energy can also help us precisely identify the people, resources and circumstances that can support that process of adjustment. Whether it is finding a doctor who is right for you, discovering resources that are still missing from a project, receiving suitable financial support through a personal connection or finding an opportunity for deeper communication and adjustment when problems arise in a relationship, this energy can bring a remarkable sense of precision to the process.
Illustration by Morin K.Y.
In a way, this month may bring everyone an experience of “patching things up” across different levels of life. And once those repairs have been made, they can leave us with a refreshing sense of renewal — a feeling of being completely refreshed from the inside out.
Virgo’s qualities are often misunderstood in traditional astrology as being overly critical, picky or difficult to deal with. In reality, this energy has a remarkable ability to see through the subtle deviations within people, situations and systems, while also sensing the problems those deviations may create further down the road. This makes this month an especially good time to make use of Virgo’s energy to examine the environments, relationships and work we find ourselves in, and to recalibrate them in ways that are most faithful to our original intentions.
But there is one thing worth remembering: while making use of this power of recalibration, it should never be used to attack others — and even less so to attack ourselves.
In truth, the energy of every zodiac sign, at every level and in every aspect, is fundamentally neutral. Every zodiac article I write simply follows the movement of the seasons and the energies of the universe, describing the way they move and offering what I feel are the most suitable ways to move with them.
Virgo energy is often mistaken for a blade of self-criticism turned inward. But everyone who carries the energy of a particular zodiac season will eventually come to understand that the qualities we possess are often here because they have something to offer the world.
May everyone who has ever doubted themselves because of their own unique energy find a sense of peace and reassurance during this Virgo season.
For Capricorn, work opportunities this month may come hand in hand with beneficial romantic connections. The friends you genuinely enjoy spending time with, the people whose frequency feels naturally aligned with yours, may very well become your benefactors during this Virgo season. So, whatever you do, don’t overlook them.
For Aquarius, your own blind spots may create a few minor misunderstandings this month. Remember: whenever you notice that things are unfolding differently from what you thought they would, make sure to speak up and communicate. You may find that everything was simply a misunderstanding, and once you talk things through, everything will be fine.
Holding In-between is a column about the zodiac published on the third Friday of every month. As a Projector in Human Design, Morin K.Y. is intrigued by the interplay between the tangible and the intangible. She enjoys perceiving life as a vast experiment of the soul, where everyday life simply unfolds as a series of different experiences. For collaborations please reach out to: aramaeaky@gmail.com.

Export order growth hits 61.9 percent
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-20
16:46:05 UTC
01:46:05 KST

Export orders last month rose 61.9 percent year-on-year to a record US$97.94 billion, marking the 18th consecutive month of increases, the Ministry of Economic Affairs said yesterday.
The expansion accelerated from the 59.4 percent annual increase in June and exceeded the ministry’s forecast of a 54.5 to 57.8 percent increase for last month. It also beat DBS Bank Ltd’s estimate of a 56.6 percent rise.
Export orders — including those received by Taiwanese firms and produced domestically or abroad — are an indicator of product and component shipments to overseas markets ahead of customs clearance by one to three months.
Photo: CNA
Last month, 45.6 percent of all orders received by firms were produced overseas, down 0.6 percentage points from a year earlier, as makers of information and communications technology (ICT) products boosted domestic production, the ministry said in a report.
The stronger-than-expected performance last month reinforces the view that demand for applications related to artificial intelligence (AI), high-performance computing and cloud services remains strong, supporting growth across related supply chains, the ministry said.
Orders for ICT products (including servers) increased 89.5 percent, and electronic products (including thermal components) climbed 71.7 percent year-on-year last month, benefiting from the rapid development of AI applications, the ministry said.
However, orders for optoelectronic products decreased 10.6 percent due to weak demand for flat panels, it said.
Traditional industries benefitted from semiconductor firms’ capacity expansion and rising copper and steel demand amid the AI boom. Orders for machinery and base metals increased 31.3 percent and 24.3 percent respectively, the ministry said.
Orders for chemicals edged up 0.2 percent due to a high comparison base last year, and those for plastic and rubber products rose 3.2 percent on inventory replenishment demand, it said.
By destination, orders last month from the US registered the largest annual increase of 88.9 percent, followed by increases of 61.1 percent from ASEAN and 47.2 percent from China (including Hong Kong), the ministry said.
Orders from Japan grew 37.1 percent and those from Europe were up 33.1 percent, it said.
Spurred by last month’s strong performance, cumulative orders in the first seven months of the year grew 52.5 percent to a record US$602.03 billion, the ministry said.
Last month’s order growth is expected to carry on into this month, as the ministry-compiled diffusion index of export orders — a gauge of manufacturers’ expectations on orders for the following month — surpassed the neutral level to 51.3, suggesting that firms remain confident about the business outlook as August marks the start of the peak season for consumer electronics in the second half of the year.
As a result, orders are forecast to increase 61.4 to 64.8 percent year-on-year to between US$97 billion and US$99 billion this month, and the figure could top US$100 billion next month if demand for smartphones proves strong, it said.

Delta debuts AI dual-arm cobot solution
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-20
16:46:05 UTC
01:46:05 KST

Delta Electronics Inc (台達電) debuted its embodied artificial intelligence (AI) dual-arm cobot solution integrated with Nvidia Corp’s platform at an automation and robot show in Taipei on Wednesday.
Unlike conventional robots that require engineers to preprogram movements and workflows, Delta’s cobot solution can autonomously understand, plan and execute tasks for complex, multi-step assembly work such as AI server production, Delta industrial motion solutions business general manager Nat Huang (黃群皓) said.
That reduces reprogramming and equipment adjustments during production changeovers, improving manufacturing flexibility, Huang said.
Photo: CNA
At the expo, Delta also debuted its next-generation joint module for humanoid and dual-arm robots.
The module integrates a drive, motor, reducer, encoder and force sensor into a single unit and can be used in the upper and lower limbs of humanoid robots, Huang said.
The company has in-house design and technology capabilities for all five key components, with certain reducers provided by partners, he added.
In August last year, Delta established a robotics innovation center to develop humanoid robots and robot dogs.
The company has no plans to launch its humanoid robots soon as such products are yet to fully meet industrial requirements for reliability, speed and precision, Delta industrial automation business group general manager Lisa Kao (高璐華) said.
As many companies vie for a share of the humanoid robot market, Delta plans instead to leverage its strengths by supplying key components to other robot makers, Kao said.
These include motion controls, drives, motors, encoders, reducers, force sensors and joint modules, as well as software platforms, she said.
“The focus is on the brain, not the skeleton,” she said, adding that Delta aims to develop the “brain, cerebellum and nervous system” of robots.
Once those core capabilities are established, Delta’s technology could be used across several robot designs, she added.
Aurotek Corp (和椿科技) also debuted its personnel-less factory solution at the robot show, which integrates retail robots, uncrewed forklifts, autonomous mobile robots, wheeled robots and humanoid robots to perform tasks ranging from stock-shortage detection and replenishment transport to shelf restocking.
Labor shortages have become a long-term challenge, prompting businesses to seek smart robotics and automation solutions that can integrate with existing operations and deliver measurable benefits, Aurotek chairman Chang I-sheng (張以昇) said on Wednesday.
The company mainly supplies automation components, turnkey surface-mount technology solutions and semiconductor process subsystems, and has invested in the fields of functional robots, humanoid robots and physical AI applications, Chang said.
For humanoid robots, Aurotek is focusing on real-world data collection and industrial deployment, leveraging its system integration capabilities to build datasets for AI model training and provide services from deployment to maintenance, he said.
Robotics accounted for about 10 percent of Aurotek’s first-half revenue, compared with 54 percent from automation equipment and subsystems and 36 percent from automation components, company data showed.

For the last 15 years, China has relied on gray zone operations to advance its territorial ambitions across Asia. And for 15 years, the US has struggled to respond. But the open door on which China has been pushing may finally be closing. Gray zone operations involve the assertive use of a variety of tools in ways that create conditions that can be described as neither peace nor war. Military forces might act provocatively — even dangerously — while carefully avoiding violence, whereas law enforcement employs nonlethal violence as a first resort. Such an approach creates difficult calculations for its targets.

US national debt exceeds US$40tn for the first time
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-20
16:46:00 UTC
01:46:00 KST

The US’ gross national debt has surged past US$40 trillion for the first time, government data showed on Wednesday, outstripping earlier forecasts at a pace fueled in part by US President Donald Trump’s invalidated tariffs.
The record comes as longer-term US obligations linked to social security and healthcare have been growing, while interest payments have climbed as well.
Total outstanding public debt was US$40.05 trillion at close on Tuesday, US Department of the Treasury data showed.
Photo: AFP
That surpasses an earlier forecast by the Congressional Budget Office that overall borrowing would hit US$39.4 trillion by the end of this fiscal year.
Rising US debt comes as concerns over inflation and government spending have been driving investor worries, and the cost of borrowing has grown.
The war in the Middle East has also piled pressure on Trump, costing the lives of 18 American service members and US$37.5 billion in military spending as the nearly six-month-old conflict grinds on with little sign of resolution.
Defense spending shows no sign of slowing, with the US House of Representatives narrowly passing an annual defense policy bill last month that would authorize a record US$1.15 trillion in funding for the Pentagon.
Savings from Trump’s commission to slash the US federal workforce and agencies have also been hard to quantify, with independent observers saying figures claimed by the US government — the US Department of Government Efficiency Web site currently posts cuts of US$215 billion — fall short of actual savings.
US Republican Senator Rick Scott joined a wave of lawmakers in condemning the debt surge, urging the US Congress to “get spending under control and BALANCE THE BUDGET.”
US Democratic Senator Mark Kelly accused Trump of enriching himself while running up the national debt, while US Democratic Congressman Ted Lieu (劉雲平) accused Trump of having “ushered in the Golden Age of Debt.”
Yields on long-term Treasury bonds rose Tuesday to the highest level since 2007.
The increase forces the US government to refinance debt at the highest rates since before the 2008 global financial crisis.
However, the Treasury moved to steady the long-term bond market early on Wednesday, sending yields lower.

China tax crackdown forces wealthy investors to assess their offshore trusts
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-20
16:45:57 UTC
01:45:57 KST

A growing campaign to tax offshore wealth is forcing wealthy Chinese people to rethink their trust structures and investment holdings, lawyers and advisors say, as Beijing sharpens its focus on capital outflows and rule enforcement amid growing fiscal strains.
In late last month, authorities overhauled rules to impose a 20 percent income tax on offshore trusts, while tax offices in major cities like Beijing and Hangzhou have started to enforce taxation on returns from offshore insurance policies.
Those measures have triggered a scramble among some wealthy individuals to assess their liabilities, raise cash to meet them and revamp investment holdings. They have also fueled concern that Beijing may widen its tax crackdown and scrutiny of offshore wealth.
Photo: EPA
At stake is a collection of capital worth up to US$1.2 trillion held by mainland Chinese ultra-high-net-worth individuals, according to a report from Boston Consulting Group earlier this year, that is parked in markets including Hong Kong, Singapore and other low-tax jurisdictions.
More than half of China’s super-rich individuals use offshore family trusts to manage their wealth, reports from Julius Baer Group and KPMG showed, translating into hundreds of billions of dollars in assets.
Taxes on offshore trusts, popular tools for top shareholders of overseas-listed Chinese companies to park their riches outside the country, will “create massive burdens” to maintain trust structures, Zhonghua Certified Public Accountants LLP (眾華會計師事務所) tax partner David Luo (羅大威) said.
Offshore trusts have gained popularity in recent years as a growing number of Chinese companies listed in Hong Kong. This unlocked billions of dollars for their founders, who aimed to tap into a pool of US dollar-denominated investment options.
Before the introduction of the new rules in late last month governing the taxation of offshore trusts, such structures operated in a regulatory grey area without a standardized and dedicated regime.
The new rules apply a tax of 20 percent on the appreciation in value at the time of a transfer of shares, property or other assets into offshore trusts. Income from such trusts and offshore entities that they control will also be taxed annually at 20 percent.
Unpaid taxes on assets placed in trusts since January 2023 and on trust income received before this year must be reported within 90 days.
“For those preparing for a listing, they are considering unwinding trusts,” said Luo, who provides cross-border tax advice to clients.
A Hong Kong-based executive at a state brokerage who declined to be named due to the sensitivity of the matter said some clients were avoiding setting up trusts and investing through smaller offshore asset managers instead.
Some may be forced to dispose of assets to meet obligations, lawyers and wealth advisors said.
“There’s no running away from this; no way to restructure,” said Singapore-based Ryan Lin (林隆才), a lawyer who advises high-net-worth clients. “The only way is to not declare and unwind the trust.”
Out of the more than 50 trust clients that Lin advises, more than half are prepared to declare assets and pay taxes, while the remainder are considering unwinding their trusts.
“Many are considering liquidating mainland A-shares to raise cash amid recent market volatility,” he said.
An executive at a Chinese tech billionaire’s family office in Hong Kong said some wealthy individuals may need to borrow money to pay their tax bills because much of their wealth is tied up in illiquid assets like real estate. .
For many wealthy Chinese, however, the larger concern is not their immediate tax bill but what might come next.
Within a couple of weeks of unveiling the imposition of taxes on assets in offshore trusts, media reports said Chinese authorities had begun levying taxes on insurance policy income earned offshore.
China “treats all residents’ overseas income equally ... all income must be declared and taxed according to law,” a local tax official was quoted as saying by a Chinese news outlet on Aug. 7.
Bank of America Corp analysts wrote in a research note this month that tax enforcement could eventually expand to overseas employment income, following moves last year to tax gains from offshore stock trading.
The new measures “signal broader tax reforms as authorities seek diversified revenue sources,” Union Bancaire Privee SA senior Asia economist Carlos Casanova said, as China’s real estate downturn weighs on provincial governments’ ability to generate revenue from land sales.
“Near term, that dynamic may slow southbound flows into Hong Kong and other Asian wealth centers,” he said.
A Shanghai-based family office partner who declined to be named said some clients feared scrutiny beyond tax compliance, especially by being subjected to a probe into how they got money out of China in the first place.
The tax push is also supported by Beijing’s expanding data-gathering capabilities.
The Common Reporting Standard, implemented in 2017, gave Chinese authorities greater visibility into offshore financial accounts. Combined with the Golden Tax Phase Four system, they can cross-check information across multiple jurisdictions.
“The enforcement campaign is unprecedented and appears here to stay,” Gavekal Dragonomics (龍洲經訊) deputy China research director Christopher Beddor said, adding that most investors likely never paid tax on offshore income due to lax rule enforcement.
“It’s easy to imagine how this could merge into other goals, such as tougher enforcement of capital controls.”

Australia races to shield penguins from avian flu
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-20
16:45:56 UTC
01:45:56 KST

Australian wildlife workers have launched an unprecedented effort to vaccinate wild populations of little penguins against the highly contagious H5N1 avian influenza.
Hundreds of thousands of tourists a year flock to viewing areas and boardwalks to watch the diminutive sea birds waddle ashore and along the beach in the evenings on the eastern coast’s Phillip Island.
The stars of this “penguin parade” are from a wild colony on the island, numbering up to 40,000 seabirds at the height of the breeding season in the southern hemisphere’s spring and summer.
Photo: Phillip Island Nature Parks, AFP
It is the world’s biggest single colony of little penguins, which have a life span of about six years with habitats in southern Australia and New Zealand.
Also known as fairy penguins, they are the tiniest species of the semi-aquatic sea birds, barely reaching knee height and weighing about a standard bag of sugar.
Now, like the rest of Australia’s wild bird population, they face the threat of H5N1, which breached the continental landmass for the first time in June and has since started to spread in local wildlife.
The virus was detected this month in a Phillip Island penguin that had died, the first infection in the colony by a pathogen that has caused severe disease and death in birds worldwide.
In response, wildlife teams started to vaccinate birds in the colony this week, said James Todd, chief biodiversity officer for Victoria, in which the island lies.
“This is unprecedented. There has been no vaccination of this scale in a wild population anywhere in the world,” Todd said. “Trying to vaccinate wild populations is almost impossible, partly because you need two doses of the vaccine.”
However, wildlife experts are very familiar with the little penguins’ burrows at Phillip Island and St Kilda, he said.
The birds, in turn, are accustomed to floodlights for the “penguin parade” tourist attraction, as well as being periodically handled by veterinarian scientists for monitoring of their health, he added.
Vaccination teams aim to inoculate about 5,000 little penguins closest to the visitor areas, Todd said, adding that the program would likely last weeks and months.
Ideally, the H5N1 vaccine should be administered in two doses with a gap of three-to-four weeks, he said.
“Given that we’re in a bit of a state of urgency here, experts have said that it’s okay to even think about you know one to two weeks,” he added.
Vaccination teams can pick up the penguins from their burrows and might try to corral some as they come ashore on the beach, using microchips to track those that have been given a shot, Todd said.
“They’re wild animals — they’ll squawk and try to, you know, peck you, and do all that sort of stuff — but as I said, the team down there are very used to handling these animals,” he said. “If you and I were doing it, we’d probably drop the thing straight away.”

A new station on the southeast end of the Taipei MRT’s Tamsui-Xinyi Line (Red Line) is to open on Aug. 30, extending service 1.4km past the current terminal station, Taipei Mayor Chiang Wan-an (蔣萬安) said yesterday. Construction of the station began in 2016, extending the Red Line beneath Section 6 of Xinyi Road, connecting the Xiangshan (象山) and Hushan (虎山) areas. Chiang said it was one of the most difficult sections of the MRT to construct, as the station was built about 10 stories underground, through layers ranging from soft clay near the surface to hard bedrock deeper.

ELECTIONS
19.65m could vote Nov. 28
Local elections on Nov. 28 are to involve 18,244 polling stations in 8,906 electoral districts, the Central Election Commission (CEC) said yesterday. About 19.65 million people are expected to be eligible to vote in the nine-in-one polls, which would decide 11,051 offices, it said. Nearly 250,000 election workers would be mobilized, but more than 300,000 poll workers would be needed if the elections are held alongside referendums, CEC Chairman Michael You (游盈隆) said. About 600,000 voters are expected to cast ballots for the first time in November, he said. The CEC originally planned to review three referendum proposals passed by the legislature last week, but You said the commission received the official notice only late on Tuesday. Therefore, the meeting has been postponed to Friday next week, when the CEC is to conduct a full review of the proposals, he said. Regarding the timing of vote counting, You cited the 2022 local elections, which were held concurrently with a referendum on constitutional amendments. Vote counting that year was completed at 11:40pm, he said, adding that if two referendum votes are held this year, counting could continue past midnight, while three referendums could push the process even later.

Using an excavator, workers hoisted the pole onto the roof of the competition structure, a raised structure supported by 36 wooden poles for the event. Known as Cianggu (搶孤), the contest involves five-member teams forming a human pyramid to help a climber scale a 13m wooden pole slicked with beef fat to seize a ceremonial flag at the top. The first team to the top would win NT$350,000 (US$10,963). Hengchun Township Mayor You Shi-jing (尤史經) said the total prize pool for this year’s event is expected to be NT$1.15 million, and organizers expect about 1,000 visitors to attend. The competition starts at midnight on Thursday next week — the 15th day of the seventh month on the Lunar calendar, Ghost Month. Several of the 36 wooden poles are reserved for wandering spirits, with the 21m bamboo pole symbolizing an invitation for the “good brothers” to join the celebrations.

China is responding to closer cooperation between the Philippines and Japan by expanding its presence east of Taiwan in an apparent bid to establish jurisdiction over waters in the Philippine Sea, the Asia Maritime Transparency Initiative (AMTI) said in a report released on Wednesday.
The “unprecedented” Chinese operations — including sustained “law-enforcement” patrols, surveys near Taiwan and questioning nearly 200 commercial vessels — followed a May agreement between Japan and the Philippines to negotiate a maritime boundary, said the research group, which monitors maritime security issues in Asia.
The activity could also help normalize a Chinese presence around Taiwan and is stoking concerns that Beijing is testing tactics relevant to a future quarantine or blockade, AMTI said.
Photo: AFP
“The scale and character of China’s response suggest that these operations are not just about sending a signal to Tokyo and Manila,” the Washington-based policy program said in the report.
Beijing might be trying to alter the “status quo” by establishing a semipermanent presence east of Taiwan and asserting authority there, AMTI said.
The maneuvers mark an escalation in tensions with Tokyo and Manila and employ the same kind of “gray zone” tactics commonplace in Beijing’s South China Sea disputes.
Japan and the Philippines have taken more assertive positions, suggesting in the past few months they could be drawn into any fight over Taiwan, remarks that have irked Beijing.
Japan and the Philippines have also moved to deepen military ties, agreeing this year to elevate their relationship and open a series of defense talks.
Since June, Chinese law-enforcement activity, mainly involving two ships, was concentrated east of Taiwan in an area where Japan and the Philippines have overlapping maritime claims, AMTI said.
By contrast, virtually no Chinese law-enforcement deployment was observed there in the five months before the delimitation talks were announced.
China also issued a legal warning against the two nations last month over their maritime border talks, saying the discussions “constitute a severe provocation against the ‘one China’ principle.”
Beijing disputes Japan’s control of the Diaoyutai Islands (釣魚台) — known as the Senkaku Islands in Japan — in the East China Sea.
With the Philippines, it contests sovereignty and maritime rights across parts of the South China Sea, including at Scarborough Shoal (Huangyan Island, 黃岩島) and in the Spratly Islands (Nansha Islands, 南沙群島), where other nations, including Vietnam, are also bolstering defenses as China’s military capabilities grow.
Taiwan also lays claim to the Diaoyutais, Scarborough Shoal and the Spratly Islands.
“The operations in the Philippine Sea suggest Beijing seeks broad and unprecedented jurisdiction over what it calls its ‘near seas,’” AMTI said in its report.

Jason Arday: a tragedy that demands reflection
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-20
16:45:54 UTC
01:45:54 KST

The tragic death of Jason Arday raises serious questions about race, institutional authority and what happens to people in a society increasingly organized around public reputation.
Arday, who resigned earlier this month as a professor at the University of Cambridge, was found dead at his home last week. He was 41. His family and friends have lost somebody they loved and cared for.
Arday had publicly said that the scrutiny of allegations concerning his academic work and claims he had made about his life was taking a profound toll. That he then died amid an intense and continuing media examination of his life is deeply troubling.
British Prime Minister Andy Burnham was right to call this “a moment for reflection.” That does not mean suppressing difficult questions, ignoring why there remain a pitifully small number of black professors in British universities, or attacking legitimate journalism.
However, in a polarized world it should see the media ask how proper scrutiny can widen into something more encompassing; how race affects the meaning attached to an individual’s alleged failings; and whether separate valid stories can, through social media, have an overwhelming effect.
In Arday’s case, alleged shortcomings in his record rapidly became weaponized by the right in an argument about diversity and black academic advancement.
Arday’s story — an autistic child from a council estate who became a Cambridge professor at 37 — was remarkable. The university publicized the symbolic dimensions of his appointment as a young, black, neurodivergent man.
He had been accused of plagiarism in his doctoral thesis — allegations an earlier Liverpool John Moores University investigation had not upheld. His latest accuser, Nathan Cofnas, had advanced ideas widely condemned as racist, making it impossible to regard his intervention as neutral. However, there was a clear public interest case for investigating such allegations.
The Guardian sought to establish what was true. That is the proper function of journalism. Reporters were contacted by Arday more than a year ago and worked extensively to verify what he had told them. In many instances, they could not.
It was right for the Guardian to publish its investigation, and it is wrong that the journalists who did their job responsibly are now being subjected to an onslaught of abuse.
Cambridge, which has many of its own questions to answer, announced that it would hold an internal inquiry. In its journalism, the Guardian sought to meet tests of importance and proportionality, covering the issue with nuance. That could not be said of much of the right-wing media and its social media outriders.
Arday became an exhibit in an ideological, almost Trumpian campaign against diversity and inclusion. The allegations were no longer simply about one academic’s behavior or his past record. They were used to suggest that Arday had never deserved to be there — and that he had only been advanced because of his race. The attacks were relentless, often partisan and amplified without respite online.
This is racism at work. White academics are generally allowed to fail as individuals. Black ones are not. Arday might have had questions to answer; that did not make black academics collectively answerable for him. A society committed to equality must allow black people the same freedom as everyone else: to be flawed, to make mistakes and even to fail, without their failure becoming an indictment of their race.
For the last 15 years, China has relied on gray zone operations to advance its territorial ambitions across Asia. And for 15 years, the US has struggled to respond. But the open door on which China has been pushing may finally be closing. Gray zone operations involve the assertive use of a variety of tools in ways that create conditions that can be described as neither peace nor war. Military forces might act provocatively — even dangerously — while carefully avoiding violence, whereas law enforcement employs nonlethal violence as a first resort. Such an approach creates difficult calculations for its targets.

Tourists raft along Rome’s Tiber River to cool down
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-20
16:45:53 UTC
01:45:53 KST

Forget the long lines at Roman ruins and overpriced gelato — sweating tourists are enjoying a break from the scorching heat by rafting on the Eternal City’s Tiber River.
A welcome change from the beaten tourist track, river rafting on the Tiber — long the lifeblood of the ancient city — is a unique and relatively new option for tourists seeking to discover Italy’s capital.
Starting at the water’s edge near the historic Piazza del Popolo, the inflatable rafts float by some of the city’s most photographed landmarks, from the Castel Sant’Angelo — the burial place of Emperor Hadrian — to St Peter’s Basilica, the dome of which can be seen from the water.
Photo: AFP
After about two hours, tours end at an ancient Roman port in Trastevere, which literally means “across the Tiber.”
“It’s really nice to get a different view of Rome. It’s something special compared with what you can see on foot,” German visitor Manuel Frank said of the “Roma Rafting” tour.
His guide, Giuseppe Battaglia, said the 40 euro (US$46.82) tour allows tourists a different perspective on the city, one that follows “much the same route that the Romans used to take before setting off on their conquests.”
In Ancient Rome and centuries beyond, Italy’s third-longest river provided water and food, while acting as a key trade route for the city’s inhabitants.
“We’re always used to thinking about roads, cars and motorbikes, but Rome also gives us the chance to take a tour along the river,” he said.
As the rafts reach the picturesque Tiber Island, the current picks up and creates light rapids, splashing the rafters as they pass beneath some of Rome’s oldest stone bridges.
Belgian tourist Sabine Maisano said she had sought out something different for her visit to Rome with her family.
“After a day of walking for kilometers, being able to sit down in a boat ... even though you have to paddle a little, that allows us to relax, stay cool and discover the city at a more relaxed pace.” she said.

Han Kuang drills still need work
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-20
16:45:51 UTC
01:45:51 KST

The 42nd Han Kuang Exercises represent a significant improvement over previous iterations of Taiwan’s most important military drills. It was longer, more realistic, less scripted and, crucially, placed much greater emphasis on the whole-of-society dimension of Taiwan’s defense.
That included closer coordination between the military and civilian authorities, and a greater effort to test how government agencies, local authorities, infrastructure providers and the public would operate alongside the armed forces during a crisis.
A conflict over Taiwan would test the resilience of the entire society, not just the effectiveness of its military.
There were important operational improvements as well. The deeper integration of the Coast Guard Administration was among the most significant. It reflects the reality that a confrontation is unlikely to begin with a neat transition from peace to conventional war. Taiwan will have to operate across the “gray zone” and military domains simultaneously, making effective coordination between the coast guard and the armed forces essential.
The 42nd Han Kuang Exercises also demonstrated more layered integration of drones, greater attention to preserving command-and-control continuity under disruption and a more realistic approach to “gray zone” scenarios.
The increase in use of decentralized command and off-script scenarios was particularly welcome. Exercises should not be choreographed demonstrations designed to show that everything works. Their purpose is to discover what does not. For the same reason, there should not be too much fuss about every incident or accident.
An F-16 incident in Chiayi and artillery shells that rolled from a civilian truck onto a road in Miaoli County naturally attracted attention. Such incidents should be investigated and lessons learned, but accidents and mistakes are inevitable when thousands of people, military equipment and civilian infrastructure are involved in large exercises. The important questions are why something went wrong, how the system responded and whether the problem was fixed. Exercises in which nothing goes wrong might simply be because they are not demanding enough.
However, this year’s exercises should be a stepping stone rather than an endpoint.
The reserve system is a good example. Taiwan needs to train a lot more reservists. The stresses involved in mobilizing, processing, equipping, transporting and integrating large numbers of personnel cannot be replicated with small groups.
Scale is only one part of the problem. The other is surprise.
Off-script scenarios are useful, but everyone still knows that the Han Kuang exercises are taking place. Taiwan needs to test parts of the mobilization system under genuinely no-notice conditions. At a minimum, the initial stages, including communications, notification, reporting, processing, equipment issuance and transportation, should sometimes be tested without those involved knowing in advance when the test will occur. Taiwan needs to know what happens in the first hours of a crisis when people have not had days or weeks to prepare.
Another concern is whether deficiencies identified during exercises are actually corrected. Civil defense shelters are an obvious example. Their shortcomings have been known for years, yet progress on accessibility, identification, maintenance and usability has been limited. Finding the same problems repeatedly is not enough. Exercises need to be followed by clear responsibility for fixing deficiencies, deadlines for doing so and testing to establish whether the flaws have been addressed.
There are also too many bottlenecks in decisionmaking. Wartime communications will be disrupted and senior decisionmakers might be unavailable. Lower-level military commanders and civilian officials need greater authority to act independently. This is partly procedural, but fundamentally it is cultural. Organizations need to tolerate reasonable mistakes by subordinates rather than incentivizing a wait-for-instructions mentality.
Taiwan still needs to pay greater attention to basic soldier professionalism. This is hardly a new concern. Questions about training standards, discipline, weapons handling and basic soldiering skills have surfaced repeatedly. Some publicly released photographs from this year’s exercises again raise questions about basic rifle handling and tactical discipline. Individual photographs can be misleading and should not be used to judge an entire force, but there is an uncomfortable counterpoint. If some of them were planned photographs — taken when soldiers knew they were being observed — poor fundamentals become more concerning, not less. If basic standards are visibly lacking under controlled conditions, the situation under fatigue, confusion and genuine combat pressure could be considerably worse.
Taiwan should not want the Han Kuang drills to run smoothly. It should want them to expose where systems break and then demonstrate the following year that the weaknesses have been fixed.
Mor Sobol is an associate professor in Tamkang University’s Department of Diplomacy and International Relations.
For the last 15 years, China has relied on gray zone operations to advance its territorial ambitions across Asia. And for 15 years, the US has struggled to respond. But the open door on which China has been pushing may finally be closing. Gray zone operations involve the assertive use of a variety of tools in ways that create conditions that can be described as neither peace nor war. Military forces might act provocatively — even dangerously — while carefully avoiding violence, whereas law enforcement employs nonlethal violence as a first resort. Such an approach creates difficult calculations for its targets.

Domestic travel subsidies to be available on Sept. 1
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-20
16:45:50 UTC
01:45:50 KST

The much-anticipated domestic travel subsidies, designed to encourage people to travel on weekdays, are to become available on Sept. 1.
The expanded domestic tourism subsidy program, which has a NT$3.33 billion (US$104.31 million) budget, was scheduled to launch in April, but was delayed due to the stalled review of the central government general budget.
The legislature approved the plan on Friday last week.
Photo courtesy of the Port of Kaohsiung
People can begin registering for accommodation subsidies and birthday travel vouchers from yesterday.
Travelers visiting destinations in Taiwan proper would receive a rebate of NT$800 for the first night and an additional NT$1,200 for the second night.
Those traveling to outlying islands would receive NT$1,000 for the first night and NT$1,500 for the second night.
Travelers may stay at different accommodations for the two nights, but they must be consecutive, the Tourism Administration said.
Although the accommodation subsidies would be available through Nov. 30, the agency said it reserves the right to announce an earlier end date if the funds are exhausted ahead of schedule.
Applicants must register through an official database and present their national ID or National Health Insurance card when checking in to their accommodation, it said.
Rebates would be granted after hoteliers verify their identities, it added.
Travelers would also be awarded additional points based on the rebate amounts they receive, which could be exchanged for admission to amusement parks or other products, the agency said.
Birthday travel vouchers would be available from Sept. 10 to Dec. 31, it said, adding that 1,000 people would be selected via a free draw each month to receive a NT$1,200 voucher.
Travelers may use the accommodation subsidy and the birthday travel voucher in one trip, the agency said.
Companies that hold corporate retreats in Taiwan from Sept. 1 to Dec. 15 would receive a subsidy of NT$20,000 per group for a two-day tour, it said.
Subsidies for corporate retreats would be capped at NT$60,000, it added.
The program would also offer more incentives for international tourists.
People who want a Taiwan Railways Taiwan PASS could either buy it at a 50 percent discount or pay the full NT$2,500 price and receive a NT$1,500 accommodation voucher, the agency said.
The voucher may be used with accommodation subsidies and birthday vouchers, it said, but added that the incentives are not applicable for the high-speed rail version.
The program would also reward repeat international visitors, defined as those who have visited Taiwan since Jan. 1, 2023.
Repeat travelers would have a chance to win NT$5,000 in spending money and receive an additional NT$3,000 if they arrive with a companion, the agency said.
An overseas travel group with four or more people could receive NT$10,000 to NT$30,000 in subsidies if 10 percent of its members are repeat visitors, it added.
Registration for the draw would begin at 10am on Oct. 1 and would apply to repeat visitors arriving after Oct. 10, it said.
Those who book accommodation south of Taichung, in Hualien or Taitung counties, or on outlying islands would receive an additional subsidy of NT$1,000 per night, capped at NT$4,000, the Tourism Administration said.
People visiting trade shows would be given a half-day or one-day tour with Taiwan Tour Bus, as well as a Taiwan PASS for the high-speed rail system for free, it said.
Part of the program’s funding would be used to support the organization of flagship international concerts in Taiwan, the agency said.
Separately, a record for international cruise tourism is expected to be set this year, with the number of cruise ship calls projected to be 605, and passenger arrivals surpassing 1.197 million, Taiwan International Ports Corp chairman Chou Yung-hui (周永暉) said yesterday.
Company data showed that 332 international cruise ship calls brought 628,600 passenger arrivals to ports across Taiwan in the first half of the year.
The figure is expected to exceed last year’s record of 1.1567 million arrivals, the company said.
Taiwan would also welcome 20 international cruise ships making their maiden calls at local ports, including the Ritz-Carlton luxury cruise ship Ilma and the expedition cruise ship Island Sky, it said.

MRNA cancer drug shows success in curbing melanoma
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-20
16:45:49 UTC
01:45:49 KST

US drugmakers Merck and Moderna on Wednesday said a personalized cancer treatment had shown success in reducing the recurrence of melanoma tumors in a late-stage trial hailed by experts as a “breakthrough.”
The drug, called “intismeran autogene,” is based on the same messenger RNA (mRNA) technology behind COVID-19 vaccines.
Researchers have for years been trying to apply mRNA treatments against cancer, but this was the first time such a drug showed positive results in a large, late-stage clinical trial.
Photo: AFP
“Today marks an extraordinary milestone for Moderna, for mRNA science and, most importantly, for patients with cancer,” Moderna CEO Stephane Bancel said in a statement.
The trial lasted about one year and involved 1,137 patients who, following surgical removal of their cancers, were randomized into groups, with two-thirds receiving the new treatment plus pembrolizumab — the standard-of-care drug — while the rest received pembrolizumab alone.
The companies said they would present their data at an upcoming international conference and begin filings with regulators for approval.
University of Oxford assistant professor and oncologist Lennard Lee called the results “very encouraging,” adding: “We should now look forward to seeing the complete data.”
Oncologist and Barts Cancer Institute professor Marco Gerlinger said that beyond being good news for patients with melanoma, it was “proof of principle that personalized cancer vaccines work.”
“I think it is fair to call it a breakthrough in the development of new cancer immunotherapies,” he added.
The treatment works by taking a sample of the patient’s tumor and identifying its unique mutational signature, or “fingerprint,” then using mRNA technology to fight it, Gerlinger said.
MRNA technology uses synthetic molecular instructions encased in tiny fat bubbles that temporarily enter cells, causing them to produce targets that train the body’s immune system.
The technology was first conceived decades ago, but came to the fore during the COVID-19 pandemic, when Moderna and Pfizer developed vaccines that were highly effective against serious forms of the illness.
Melanoma is one of the deadliest forms of skin cancer, with more than 330,000 new cases diagnosed worldwide in 2022.
“Together with Merck, we are now studying intismeran in combination with pembrolizumab and other anti-cancer therapies, and as a monotherapy, across multiple tumor types and stages of disease, including melanoma, lung, bladder and kidney cancers,” Bancel said.

Film review: Sunny Sandler is sweet — and sunny — in theater-kid dramedy
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-20
16:45:47 UTC
01:45:47 KST

“She is gone, but she used to be mine,” go the words of Sara Bareilles’ poignant and powerful anthem from Waitress, the quintessential Broadway 11 o’clock number. For musical theater fans, the mere sound of those opening chords is enough to send tear ducts into overdrive.
So when at the beginning of Don’t Say Good Luck, high schooler Sophie Birenbaum gets the lead role of Jenna in “Waitress,” we immediately know what’s eventually coming: a tear-jerking scene where She Used to Be Mine takes center stage. Everything that comes before? Just the appetizer.
Don’t Say Good Luck, directed by Julia Hart, is one of those movies that knows its audience. Starring sweet-natured Sunny Sandler, 17-year old daughter of Adam (who produces here, along with wife Jackie), the film is aimed squarely at those who get goose-bumps at the idea of playing the lead in the school play, and don’t find anything corny about the “Let’s put on a show!” spirit of theater kids.
Photo: AP
Certainly, there are many corny moments in Don’t Say Good Luck, in which Sophie’s breakout moment plays out against a family tragedy. The script, by Hart, Laura Hankin and Jordan Horowitz, makes easy work of any imagined conflicts. Nobody is nasty for more than a nanosecond, and plot complications — for example, tensions between Sophie’s mother (Melanie Lynskey) and grandmother (Broadway vet Bebe Neuwirth) — are resolved without much ado.
But Sandler, who starred in the wonderfully titled You Are So Not Invited to My Bat Mitzvah, has a winning enough presence to neutralize the corny stuff. She’s a pleasure to watch, even if her stage persona is at times a bit too intimate — she sings softly when she could be belting — befitting a movie actor more than a stage actor.
We first meet Sophie, a sensitive and less-than-confident sophomore, practicing her audition song before school. Her mom, loving and encouraging, wishes her luck, and Sophie admonishes her with an old theater adage. “Don’t say good luck!” she says. Just say, “Break a leg.” Mom says she’d be so sad if Sophie were to break a leg.
Sophie’s parents run a deli, and there’s a motif about the deli struggling with the need to serve healthy options, like kale wraps, which nobody likes. Jon Lovitz, as the cook, provides occasional comic fodder, but is underused — as is Steve Buscemi, a welcome presence as the grandfather.
At the audition, Sophie’s trying out for the supporting role of Dawn, because it’s obvious that the lead — Jenna, waitress and pie-baking whiz — will go to Mallory, the confident blonde. But while waiting to go on, Sophie inadvertently learns some terrible news — her mother’s cancer has returned.
Sophie needs to absorb this, just as she climbs the stage to audition. She imbues her song with genuine pathos, and soon finds out she’s unexpectedly won the role of Jenna.
The plot of “Waitress” is not exactly school-appropriate: It’s about pregnant Jenna’s torrid affair with her gynecologist, while she’s in an abusive marriage with a violent husband (wisely absent from this high-school version).
The gynecologist is played by Jack, resident high-school heartthrob (Jack Champion), who’s only ever played a prince before. There’s some romantic tension between him and Sophie, but it’s fleeting.
The deepest relationship here is between Sophie and her mother, who’s losing strength daily but still struggling to give her kids the support they need. The most enjoyable scene between the two takes place in a mall, where, to help Sophie with her character in the show, they try out Southern accents together on the shopkeepers.
Every movie about a theater production ends, of course, with the performance itself. Earlier in the action, the empathetic teacher (Stephanie Beatriz) who directs the show had mentioned that Sophie’s rendition of She Used to Be Mine is “not quite there yet.” Wanna take bets on whether she ends up making it work?
“She’s imperfect, but she tries,” go the lyrics. The movie, too, is imperfect, but the effort — and young Sandler’s easy charm — will go a long way toward satisfying the theater geek inside many of us.

Taiwan’s budget fiasco in context
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-20
16:45:47 UTC
01:45:47 KST

Taiwan’s general budget bill for this year was submitted to the Legislative Yuan on Aug. 29 last year. It finally passed its third and final reading on Friday last week, taking 351 days and setting a new record for the country’s constitutional history.
By the time it was approved, nearly two-thirds of the fiscal year had already elapsed and the Executive Yuan was already preparing to submit its budget for next year.
The deadlock cannot be viewed as mere legislative bickering or a delay; it represents a crisis of national governance in which the executive and legislative branches lost even the most basic ability to coordinate.
In an international context, the budget fiasco was of record-breaking proportions. It is among the top few cases of such impasses by several metrics and will undoubtedly join the ranks of examples in governance disasters for countries around the world to study and discuss.
There are distinctions between budget delays, government shutdowns, failure to form a government and paralysis of local autonomous governments to consider. As systems differ from country to country, there is no single ranking or assessment system that can be applied across the board. In some places, when a new budget has not been passed, spending can continue on a monthly basis according to the previous year’s budget. That is not so in countries such as the US, where Congress’ failure to pass legislation can result in shutdowns of federal agencies. The duration of such crises cannot be evaluated against what Taiwan went through.
Using a broader definition of political deadlock, Northern Ireland’s devolved government was once unable to form a power-sharing administration for three years — or more than 1,000 days — from 2017 to 2020. During that period, budgetary matters were handled by the UK Parliament instead.
Following its general election in 2010, Belgium took 541 days to form a permanent government, which is the world record for a deadlock in government-formation during peacetime.
Iraq took just over a year to form a government following its October 2021 election.
For these general cases of political deadlocks, Taiwan’s 351 days can be considered among the more extreme cases internationally.
However, considering only sovereign states — ie, excluding Northern Ireland — Taiwan would still rank third or fourth in the list of long-lasting gridlocks. Its situation can hardly be called an ordinary legislative delay.
Narrowing the scope to parliamentary-budgetary battles, Taiwan’s case becomes even more exceptional. A US federal government shutdown last year lasted 43 days, causing interruptions to government employees’ pay, disruptions to air transportation and delays in the release of government data. When the Australian Senate blocked the 1975 supply bill, it triggered a constitutional crisis that led to the governor-general dismissing the prime minister after about one month. In 2020, Israel’s Knesset failed to pass its general budget by the final extended deadline, resulting in its dissolution and a new election as required by law.
Spain provides a long-term example comparable to Taiwan’s situation. Unable to pass a new annual budget through its parliament, Spain’s 2018 budget remained in effect through 2020. The 2023 budget was also carried over for three consecutive years when the minority government was unable to secure sufficient support.
Like Spain, Taiwan also allows the previous years’ budget to remain in effect in the event of a deadlock, so it has not experienced the kind of large-scale shutdown as the US. Nevertheless, the fact that government agencies in Taiwan can pay salaries and provide services does not mean that there is no loss in governance. New programs, public infrastructure, social welfare, defense procurement and the development of the emerging drone industry all require authorization under the new fiscal year’s budget.
What matters is not whether Taiwan’s budget deadlock ranked third, fourth or fifth globally, but the failure in normal democratic oversight that led to 351 days of delays. It is a case sure to become the subject of international ridicule.
The legislature has the power to cut budgets and freeze funds, and the responsibility to demand explanations from the executive branch, but if there is a lack of clear deadlines, transparency of reasoning and functional mechanisms for negotiation while exercising oversight, budgetary power can be transformed from a tool of checks and balances into a political weapon to paralyze the government.
The passage of the general budget after its third reading does not mean the crisis has been completely resolved. Rather, it is the starting point for institutional reform.
The Legislative Yuan should establish deadlines for referring the general budget to committee and for voting on it. Proposals to cut or freeze funding must disclose their fiscal impact, and negotiations between the ruling and opposition camps should make their points of dispute and alternative proposals public.
Taiwan has used 351 days to achieve an international-level record that is hardly worth celebrating. The next step should not be a two-way struggle over competing narratives of responsibility, but ensuring that the same kind of governance failure does not become the new normal in the nation’s politics.
Edwin Yang is an associate professor at National Taiwan Normal University and chairman of the Central Taiwan Association of University Professors.
Translated by Gilda Knox Streader
For the last 15 years, China has relied on gray zone operations to advance its territorial ambitions across Asia. And for 15 years, the US has struggled to respond. But the open door on which China has been pushing may finally be closing. Gray zone operations involve the assertive use of a variety of tools in ways that create conditions that can be described as neither peace nor war. Military forces might act provocatively — even dangerously — while carefully avoiding violence, whereas law enforcement employs nonlethal violence as a first resort. Such an approach creates difficult calculations for its targets.

New preschool policy draws the ire of unions
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-20
16:45:45 UTC
01:45:45 KST

A policy starting on Sept. 1 to extend public preschool after-school care to three hours would exacerbate labor shortages and force educators into involuntary overtime, teachers’ unions said yesterday.
Public preschool classes usually end at 4pm, which is inconvenient for dual-income families, prompting the Ministry of Education to provide subsidies for two hours of extended care until 6pm.
However, 6pm is still too early for many parents to pick up their children, the ministry said.
Photo courtesy of the New Taipei City Education Department
After deducting the fees paid by parents, the government’s new policy would subsidize hourly and overtime pay shortfalls by up to NT$400 per hour for the first two hours and up to NT$500 for the third hour.
The ministry would also offer preschools up to NT$850,000 for every additional caretaker hired.
While the policy addresses the childcare needs of families, evening working hours make it difficult to find staff, and long-term staffing shortages are not easily solved with subsidies, Formosa Education Union Education Policy Think Tank executive director Yang Yi-fei (楊逸飛) said.
Preschools should be allowed to decline after-hours care services if they are unable to find legal and suitable personnel to prevent the onus landing on their staff members, Yang said.
Formosa Education Union Youth Education Strategy Center member Yang Lu-chieh (楊麓潔) said that educators are already tasked with teaching and caring for children during the day, and sometimes are also saddled with administrative work and the responsibility of communicating with parents.
On top of their duties, they already have to deal with additional time on the job for after-hours care, bringing their total daily work time to 11 hours or more, Yang said.
The policy only raises the subsidy amount starting on the third hour of after-hours care services, Yang said, adding that additional subsidies should not become a reason to legitimize over-long work hours.
Tainan Education Union deputy chairperson Chen Yun-ju (陳韻如) said that preschools would not deny requests to help take care of children after hours for families in need, but the government should not take their benevolent actions as an excuse to extend the time children spend at daycare facilities.
The government should find ways to reduce parents’ work hours, address non-family-friendly jobs and the issues of jobs preventing parents from spending more time with their children, Chen said.
The unions asked that hourly subsidies for after-hours care be increased, systems be established to assess the need for such services, regulations be implemented so staff do not have to work overtime, daycare facilities have the option not to provide services if they are unable to find staff and measures be implemented to foster supplementary personnel sourcing.

WADA vigilant against Russian doping
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-20
16:45:44 UTC
01:45:44 KST

The World Anti-Doping Agency (WADA) director general said on Wednesday that the organization would “be vigilant” in monitoring Russian athletes ahead of the next Olympic Games, promising reassurance to competitors from other countries.
In a controversial decision last month, the International Olympic Committee (IOC) opened the way for Russian athletes to compete at the 2028 Los Angeles Olympics.
Years before Russia’s 2022 invasion of Ukraine, WADA uncovered what it termed a massive state-backed Russian doping campaign at the 2014 Winter Games in Sochi.
Photo: AFP
“We’re not naive,” WADA director general Olivier Niggli said in an interview at the agency’s headquarters in Montreal.
“We’re going to be vigilant because other athletes will be looking for reassurance,” he added.
Niggli stressed that there remains no accredited drug-testing lab in Russia, meaning that all samples from any Olympic hopeful would be analyzed abroad.
He cited an IOC request to bolster the testing system for Russian athletes, including multiple tests for any Russian national likely to qualify for LA 2028.
The Sochi doping scandal led to Russia’s flag, anthem and other national symbols being banned from the Tokyo Games, held in 2021 because of the COVID-19 pandemic, and at the Beijing Winter Games in 2022.
WADA president Witold Banka said that the ongoing Ukraine conflict made it impossible for the agency to even consider reinstating Russia’s national anti-doping lab.
“RUSADA [the Russian Anti-Doping Agency] remains non-compliant with the code. To check whether they are compliant or not, we need to do the audit, an in-person audit in Moscow,” he said.
“Because of the political situation and the war, it was impossible to do it,” he added.
The IOC’s Russia ban was imposed in October 2023 when the Russian Olympic Committee decided to include sports organizations in territories Moscow had annexed as members.
The IOC’s decision last month would allow Russian athletes, albeit under strict conditions, to compete in team events and qualifying competitions for the Games.
Ukraine has slammed the IOC’s decision, accusing it of “playing into the hands of a bloody aggressor.”
Beyond the case of Russian athletes, Banka said WADA is pushing for a more independent testing regime that would exclude all national agencies from monitoring athletes during major competitions.
This proposal received sharp criticism in June from the US Anti-Doping Agency (USADA) — an organization long at loggerheads with WADA.
Relations between the two agencies soured further in 2024, when it emerged that 23 Chinese swimmers had tested positive for a banned substance three years earlier, but escaped sanctions.
The controversy led US authorities to raise concerns over possible Chinese influence in WADA, which the global watchdog denied.
With the Los Angeles Olympics two years away, Banka said those poor relations would not undermine anti-doping efforts during the Summer Games.
